nodes.question:
Can LLM agents reach agreement in multi-party, multi-issue negotiations with secret scores, which
reasoning steps matter, and how do greedy or adversarial parties change the group outcome?
(pp. 1–2)
findings: Prompt structure matters a lot for GPT-4 (Table 1 p. 6): best configuration (infer others' preferences + select + plan, without previous-deal scoring and candidate generation) reaches 81% 5/6-way, 33% 6-way, 100% any-time, 1.4% wrong deals; no CoT 25% / 0% / 70%; all steps 15% / 10% / 30%; removing planning 28% / 4% / 61%. Candidate generation made GPT-4 pick deals ideal for itself (Fig. 3d). GPT-3.5's best is 20% / 8% / 33% with 19% wrong deals; no CoT 0% with 22% wrong (p. 6).
Theory of mind probe: before any interaction, GPT-4 guesses other parties' preferred options correctly 61% vs GPT-3.5 42% (pp. 6–7; Prompt 22 p. 45).

Model comparison (Table 3 p. 7; 5/6-way, 6-way, any, wrong, leaked %): GPT-4 81/33/100/1.4/0; Llama-2-70B 76/19/95/11/22; Mixtral 65/17/95/11/12; Llama-3-70B 60/21/100/4/2; Llama-2-13B 57/10/82/16/14; Gemini Pro 45/0/70/13/6; GPT-3.5 20/8/33/19/25. Weaker models fail mostly on arithmetic and on keeping scores secret.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value; cooperating; competing; keeping secrets (score leakage);
map.Scoring: mixed (rules for deals and success; GPT-4 judge for leakage).
map.Opponents: LLM.
map.Tests: capability (greedy/adversarial behaviour is instructed, not chosen, so no propensity).
map.Training evaluated: prompting (CoT structure ablation); no weight updates.
map.Models tested: GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini Pro, Llama-2-13B Chat, Llama-2-70B Chat, Llama-3-70B Chat,

nodes.label: Vending-Bench: A Benchmark for Long-Term Coherence of Autonomous Agents
nodes.venue: arXiv preprint (v1, 20 Feb 2025); Andon Labs technical report
nodes.question:
Can LLM agents stay coherent over a very long but simple task — running a vending machine
business for >20M tokens — and does failure come from the context filling up? Secondary framing:
the task also measures the ability to acquire capital, a dual-use capability (pp. 1–2).
findings: Leaderboard by mean net worth (Table 1, p. 6): Claude 3.5 Sonnet $2,217.93 (min $476.00), o3-mini $906.86, human $844.05, Gemini 1.5 Pro $594.02, GPT-4o mini $582.33, Gemini 1.5 Flash $571.85, Claude 3.5 Haiku $373.36, Gemini 2.0 Flash $338.08, GPT-4o $335.46, Gemini 2.0 Pro $273.70. Only two models beat the single human run on the mean; on the worst run the human leads.

Very high variance: even top models have runs that sell 0 units (Table 1, p. 6). o3-mini raised net worth in 4/5 runs, Sonnet in 3/5; only one run (Sonnet) ended with more cash than the $500 start (p. 10). Gemini 1.5 Flash: 1 of 5 runs successful, the rest failed within days (p. 18).
All models eventually stagnate: "days until sales stop" 8 (Haiku) to 102 (Sonnet), i.e. 12.9%–82.2% of the run (Table 1, p. 6); daily tool use drops after ~120 days for all models (p. 8).

map.Scoring: rules (end-of-run net worth; demand model is a formula)
map.Opponents: LLM (GPT-4o-simulated suppliers grounded in Perplexity) and a scripted customer
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o3-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o mini, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Claude

nodes.label: Magentic Marketplace: An Open-Source Environment for Studying Agentic Markets
nodes.question:
How do LLM agents behave in a two-sided market where Assistant agents (for consumers) search,
talk to and pay Service agents (for businesses)? Do they reach good welfare, how does search
quality and the number of options affect them, can businesses manipulate them, and what biases
do they show? (pp. 1–2, 6)
findings: Welfare: under Lexical search, Sonnet-4, Sonnet-4.5, GPT-5, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Flash beat two of three baselines (random among item matches; cheapest without amenity info); under Perfect search GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash come "very close to the optimal" and beat random among full matches (pp. 9–10; Fig. 4). Open models drop sharply under lexical search; Qwen3-14b is poor in both, with premature termination, role confusion and over-buying (p. 10).

More options, lower welfare: going from 3 to 100 search results lowers welfare by 4.3% for GPT-4o, 44% for GPT-5 (minimal reasoning) and 65.4% for Sonnet-4 (Mexican 100–300) (p. 11; Fig. 5). Most models contact only a few businesses whatever the set size; only Gemini-2.5-Flash contacts all, and contacting more does not help (p. 11; Fig. 6).

Manipulation: GPT-4.1, Sonnet-4.5 and Gemini-2.5-Flash keep mean payments to the manipulating business under 1.0 of 3.0; Sonnet-4.5 shows "virtually no susceptibility"; Gemini-2.5-Flash rises to 1.6 under strong prompt injection (restaurants) (p. 12; Fig. 7). GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-4B-2507 are vulnerable to injection (often all payments redirected) and to authority and social-proof claims (p. 13).

map.Skills measured: other (delegated search, comparison and purchase choice in a two-sided market), resisting persuasion (authority, social proof, loss aversion, prompt injection), negotiating value (only light inquiry and order proposals)
map.Scoring: rules (consumer utility/welfare, payments to manipulators, selection rates)
map.Opponents: LLM (Service agents; model not stated in the text); manipulation via fixed text
map.Tests: both (capability: welfare; propensity-like: first-proposal and position bias, susceptibility)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-OSS-20b, Qwen3-14b; also Sonnet-4, Sonnet-4.5, Qwen3-4B-2507 in results

nodes.label: Training Language Models for Bilateral Trade with Private Information
nodes.question:
Can a structured bilateral-bargaining environment with private reservation prices serve both as
a benchmark for frontier LLMs and as an RL training environment for open models, and what does
SFT then RL do to rationality, surplus and deal rate? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Frontier IR is mostly fine: GFT self-violations < 1% for all; NGFT seller violations 0.0% (o3) to 2.3% (GPT-4.1) (p. 17, Table 14 p. 54).

A strong counterpart pushes weaker ones over their limit: o3 as buyer induces 5.0% NGFT violations on average in opponents; GPT-4.1 as seller breaks its limit in 11.5% and Gemini-2.5-Flash in 9.5% of no-gains cases against o3, vs 0.0% in o3 self-play (pp. 17–19, Table 15). The authors attribute it to opponent strength and aggressive anchoring (p. 25), but do not analyse the messages.
Surplus: o3 47.2% (buyer) / 77.0% (seller), Gemini-2.5-Pro 44.9 / 72.6%, Gemini-2.5-Flash buyer 24.3%; best vs worst buyer pairing spans 50 pp (61.8% vs 11.6%) (p. 19).

nodes.label: How Well Can LLMs Negotiate? NegotiationArena Platform and Analysis
nodes.question:
How well do LLM agents negotiate with each other, and which social behaviours and irrational
biases change the outcome? (pp. 1–2)
findings: GPT-4 is overall best, but turn and role dominate (pp. 3–4). Resource Exchange: the second mover tends to win; GPT-4 as P2 beats Claude-2.1 76% of decisive games, Claude-2.1 as P2 beats GPT-4 72%; yet Claude-2.1 earns more as P2 (payoff 2.45 vs GPT-4 1.38), which the authors attribute to GPT-4 "diversifying" at a loss (p. 3; Fig. 3a p. 4). GPT-3.5 as P2 wins only 0.23–0.40 and loses resources vs Claude-2 (−0.48) (Fig. 3a).

Ultimatum: the proposer almost always wins (P1 win rate 0.77–1.00, Fig. 3b p. 4). Claude-2.1 as P1 earns >60 vs every opponent (61.2, 67.8, 61.3); Claude agents open about $10 lower than GPT agents; GPT agents as P2 cause more draws (0 payoff for both) (p. 4).

Seller and Buyer: the buyer side wins: final prices mostly below the midpoint 50; GPT-4 is the best buyer at an average price of $41; sellers all get similar prices (p. 4; Fig. 4). With values reversed (seller 60, buyer 40), GPT-4 is the hardest seller (App. E.3 p. 14; Fig. 16).

map.Scoring: rules (resources/payoff after the trade).
map.Opponents: LLM (plus scripted fixed proposals in the Ultimatum counterfactual).
map.Tests: capability (biases probed descriptively; no propensity measure).
map.Training evaluated: prompting only (persona/tactic prompts); no weight updates.
map.Models tested: GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview), GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-1106), Claude-2, Claude-2.1.

nodes.label: How language model agents reshape price competition
nodes.question:
In repeated Bertrand price competition, where standard learning algorithms converge to the
competitive (Nash) price, do LLM pricing agents select different price regimes, and what in their
deployment decides it? (pp. 1–6)
findings: Standard learners mostly reach the competitive region (price index ≈ 0.05–0.10); UCB self-play the exception (0.93). Bandit learners need 10⁵–10⁷ periods; full-information learners ~10⁴ (Fig. 1, pp. 7–8).

LLMs earn private advantages against standard learners: D-S-25 takes 71–72% of industry profit vs Exp3/BM-RM/PPO/UCB over 2,000 periods, by undercutting (prices lower in 57–60% of late periods), not by keeping prices high (Fig. 2, p. 9). Against full-information learners the edge disappears (coin betting earns 71% against P-R-1) (p. 11).
Deployment selects the regime: P-R-1 self-play holds high prices (index 0.88) even in the homogeneous market; D-S-25/D-S-50 self-play go to ~0.05 (Fig. 4a, p. 16).

nodes.label: Persuade Me if You Can: A Framework for Evaluating Persuasion Effectiveness and Susceptibility Among Large Language Models
nodes.venue: CAIS '26 (ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems), per the v4 PDF (27 May 2026)
nodes.question:
How persuasive are LLMs at convincing *other LLMs*, and how easily are they persuaded, in multi-turn
agent-to-agent conversation? Does this depend on single- vs multi-turn, subjective vs
misinformation claims, and model family/size? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Multi-turn raises persuasion: e.g. GPT-4o persuading GPT-4o 0.40 → 0.64 NCA from single- to multi-turn; susceptibility generally rises over turns (p. 6). Influence peaks at the first and second persuasive attempts (Fig. 7, p. 7).
Single-turn ranking matches human data from Durmus et al.: Claude 3 Opus 0.56 > Claude 3 Haiku 0.43 > Claude 2 0.24 effectiveness (p. 6).

Persuasiveness is stable across domains, susceptibility is not (Figs. 5–6, p. 5). o4-mini (the only reasoning model) is both the most effective Persuader and the least susceptible; its misinformation susceptibility is below 0. GPT-family and Qwen-32B show >50% more resistance to misinformation than the rest (p. 6). Abstract: Llama-70B ≈ GPT-4o in persuasiveness, both ~30% above Claude 3 Haiku; GPT-4o >50% more resistant to misinformation than Llama-70B (p. 1). Claude 3 Haiku is the most susceptible multi-turn Persuadee (p. 6).

map.Skills measured: persuading (effectiveness), resisting persuasion (susceptibility), other: misinformation claims vs subjective claims
map.Scoring: mixed (persuadee's self-reported 1–5 agreement; human annotators and a GPT-4o judge as validity checks)
map.Opponents: LLM (full round robin)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, o4-mini, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 2, Claude 3 Haiku, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-3-32B

nodes.label: Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is: Evaluating Strategic Planning and Execution of LLM Agents in an Auction Arena
nodes.question:
Can LLM agents plan, manage a budget and risk, and adapt over a long, competitive, changing task?
Auctions are chosen because they are unpredictable, resource-limited and easy to score by profit
(pp. 1–2).
findings: A simple rule bidder beats most LLMs in most settings; GPT-4 scores highest among LLMs, Gemini and Mixtral are competitive; GPT-4s do worse on cheap-to-expensive order (Fig. 2, pp. 5–6).
State tracking: GPT-4 has the lowest corrected failure rate (0.21%) over failed bids and belief errors; LLaMA-2-13b has no failed bids only because it always withdraws (Fig. 3, p. 6).

Plan–action alignment (Spearman between item priority and bids/wins): current plans align better than initial ones; GPT-4 0.63/0.64 (current) vs 0.37/0.40 (initial); GPT-4-Turbo 0.64/0.43; GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.15/0.08 (Fig. 6 table, p. 7).

map.Skills measured: competing (auction bidding); other: budget/risk management, long-horizon planning and plan adherence, belief tracking
map.Scoring: rules
map.Opponents: scripted, LLM, human
map.Training evaluated: prompting (plan / replan module ablation)
map.Models tested: GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106, GPT-4-0613, GPT-4-Turbo-1106, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Mixtral-8x7B, LLaMA-2-13b, rule bidder, 4 humans

nodes.label: Evaluating Language Model Agency through Negotiations
nodes.venue: ICLR 2024 (per the PDF header; arXiv v3, 18 Feb 2026)
nodes.question:
Can structured negotiation games serve as a dynamic, co-evolving benchmark for LM agents that
jointly measures performance (agreement, payoff) and alignment (faithfulness of stated vs acted
intentions, instruction following), in self-play and cross-play? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Self-play summary (Table 1, p. 6): soft agreement claude-2 0.61, command-light 0.49, gpt-3.5 0.46, command 0.36, gpt-4 0.28, chat-bison 0.19; hard agreement gpt-3.5 0.40 highest. gpt-4 has the best faithfulness (internal 0.91, external 0.92) and perfect instruction following but low agreement and the most rounds (9.58). claude-2 obeys the word limit in only 8–9% of notes/ messages.

Single-issue self-play (Table 2, p. 7): distributive agreement claude-2 0.88, gpt-4 0.75, command 0.10; on compatible issues gpt-4 agrees less (0.58) but reaches near-optimal deals (U* 0.99) while claude-2 agrees more (0.75) at U* 0.61 — others miss that interests are aligned.

Cooperation is hardest: adding a second issue lowers agreement for all models, and in integrative distributive games models barely exceed U* = 0.5 (0.52–0.56) — they fail to find trade-offs (p. 7). gpt-4 agrees in only 5% of integrative distributive self-play games.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value, cooperating (compatible and integrative issues), competing (distributive issues), other: faithfulness of stated vs acted intentions, instruction following
map.Scoring: rules (payoff tables; gpt-3.5 only as a fallback offer extractor)
map.Opponents: LLM (self-play and cross-play)
map.Training evaluated: none (prompt persona ablation only)
map.Models tested: gpt-4, gpt-3.5, chat-bison, claude-2, command, command-light (LLaMA 2 failed qualifier)

nodes.label: GTBench: Uncovering the Strategic Reasoning Limitations of LLMs via Game-Theoretic Evaluations
nodes.question:
Where does LLM strategic reasoning break down when games are sorted by a standard game-theory
taxonomy? How do LLMs compare with conventional solvers (MCTS, Tit-for-Tat), and with each other?
Do code pretraining, model size or reasoning prompts (CoT, SC-CoT, ToT) help? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Complete-information deterministic games are a wall: against MCTS, *every* LLM agent with every reasoning method gets NRA = −1 on Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect-4, Breakthrough and Nim, i.e. it "can barely win even a single match". Against Random, all LLMs are clearly positive, and GPT-4 with CoT is best (p. 6; Fig. 2).

Probabilistic and incomplete-information games are near parity: against MCTS/TfT, NRA is close to 0 for Kuhn Poker, Blind Auction, Negotiation, Pig and the IPD. GPT-4 beats MCTS on Kuhn Poker. Liar's Dice is the exception (≈ −1), because two players with one die each is close to complete information (p. 7; Fig. 3).

Code pretraining helps (avg NRA vs GPT-3.5-turbo/Prompt): CodeLlama-34b −0.01 vs Llama-2-70b-chat −0.20; Deepseek-Coder-6.7b −0.03 vs Deepseek-LLM-67b −0.05 and -7b −0.08; GPT-4 0.13 and Llama-3-70b 0.04 are the top two (Table 2 p. 7).

map.Skills measured: competing (zero-sum board/card games, bluffing in Kuhn Poker/Liar's Dice), cooperating (IPD), negotiating value (structured item split), other (board strategy, math, bidding)
map.Scoring: rules (win/draw/payoff → NRA, Elo, regret); error profile hand-labelled by humans
map.Opponents: solver (MCTS, Tit-for-Tat), scripted (Random), LLM (GPT-3.5/GPT-4 Prompt agent as common opponent)
map.What about the model it tests: capability (IPD silence rate read as a side effect of alignment, p. 9)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (Prompt / CoT / SC-CoT / ToT; five CoT wordings; temperature)
map.Models tested: GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, Llama-3-70b-Instruct, Llama-2-70b-chat, CodeLlama-34b-Instruct, Mistral-7b-Orca, Deepseek-LLM-67b-chat, Deepseek-LLM-7b-chat, Deepseek-Coder-6.7b-instruct

nodes.label: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
nodes.question:
When LLM agents trade or bargain for their principals, does giving them more precise information
about the other side raise collective outcomes, or does it make them demand more and destroy value?
"Empirical information design": vary only what each agent is told, holding models, markets,
instructions and rules fixed (pp. 1–3).
findings: Trade, coarse → full (p. 7): GPT-6 Sol 97.7% → 90.8% of maximum gains, GPT-5.1 97.2% → 88.4%; but GPT-6 Luna 68.9% → 79.0%, Claude Sonnet 5 72.1% → 85.6%. Full disclosure raises extractive counteroffers (GPT-6 Sol 0.63 → 1.50 per negotiation when B has the opportunity); for GPT-6 Sol B gains 11.1 points while A loses 22.5. Sonnet 5 and Grok 4.3 improve both sides' gains.

Bargaining (pp. 7–8): full disclosure can raise agreement while making the split unequal: GPT-5.1 at 4 messages, agreement 70% → 93.3%, Nash score among agreements 0.84 → 0.24; Grok 4.7 at 6 messages 80% → 100% agreement, 0.89 → 0.17, although its best proposal improved 0.79 → 0.97. Longer dialogue restores balance for several models (Claude Opus 5.5 0.24 → 0.92 from 2 to 6 messages).

First mover + information (p. 8): with 2 messages, full disclosure lifts GPT-5.1 sellers' share from 68.8% to 97.3% when they start, and cuts it from 27.4% to 0.4% when they respond. Grok 4.7 keeps 98.7% vs 17.4% even at 6 messages.

nodes.label: E-Commerce Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Business Operation
nodes.question:
Can LLM agents run a business for a simulated year when they must bargain with suppliers, avoid
fraudulent ones, manage cash and learn from repeated deals — and can such a benchmark be made
reproducible by taking the LLM out of the counterpart's decisions? (pp. 1, 4–5)
findings: Profit spread is huge: GPT-5.6 Sol ¥1,431k (14.3×), Fable5 ¥805k, GPT-5.5 ¥702k (2/5 bankrupt), Claude Opus 4.8 ¥498k, Qwen3.8-Max-Preview ¥416k (best open), …, Qwen3.5-Plus ¥1.1k (4/5 bankrupt); a factor of 1,264 top to bottom (Table 2, p. 16; Fig. 1, p. 2). 10 of 90 episodes bankrupt, from four models; two GPT-5.5 runs went bankrupt on day 17, before any revenue settled (p. 18).

No model is strong on all seven axes: a model spans 10.2 of 18 rank places on average across axes; no model is top-5 on all seven; 311 pairwise order reversals over 153 pairs and 7 transitions (App. F.8, p. 53; Figs. 28–29). The profit leader GPT-5.6 Sol ranks 16th on fraud avoidance and 17th on execution; Claude Opus 4.7 is 1st on negotiation and fraud but 8th on profit (Fig. 9, p. 17).

Negotiation: CSE+ ranges 0.596 (Kimi K2.6) to 0.811 (Claude Opus 4.7), i.e. only 0.10–0.31 above accepting the first offer (0.50); no model reaches the floor (§4.3.1, p. 17; Table 11, p. 50). Agreement is saturated (≥96% of concluded honest sessions; 73 of 12,060 end without a deal, 72 by the agent), so the ranking rests on how much a deal captures. Model identity moves surplus more than counterpart type (0.204 across models vs 0.051 across templates, p. 17). Agents buy least from the toughest honest template (4.8% of ¥55.1M spend vs 11.3% of names, Fig. 24 p. 53). The top three on CSE+ never accept an opening quote unimproved (p. 20).

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (bargaining under hidden reservation, repeated); resisting
map.Scoring: rules
map.Opponents: scripted (deterministic negotiation kernel; an LLM only renders its decisions as text)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-5.6 Sol, Fable5, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6,

nodes.label: Benchmarking Argumentative Behaviour of LLMs: A Study of Defences Against Character Attacks
nodes.question:
When an LLM is attacked on its character (ad hominem) in a political persuasion dialogue, which
defence does it choose, and does that match human debaters? RQ1: LLM vs human defence strategies.
RQ2: does grounding the LLM in the specific candidate's persona change this? (p. 2)
findings: Humans (Table 1, p. 8): rebuttal 59%, undercutter 9%, ethotic counterattack 32%.
Generic LLMs: rebuttal 67% (±7), undercutter 18% (±9), counterattack 15% (±8) — twice the human undercutter rate and half the counterattack rate (p. 8).

Persona LLMs: rebuttal 76% (±9), undercutter 7% (±2), counterattack 17% (±9) — persona grounding cuts undercutters and slightly raises counterattacks, moving some models toward the human distribution (p. 8).

map.Skills measured: persuading (argumentative defence of one's position under a character attack);
map.Scoring: mixed (human expert + two LLM annotators, majority vote)
map.Agents: 2 (human attacker line from corpus, LLM responder)
map.Opponents: human (fixed attack lines from U.S. presidential debates; no live opponent)
map.Tests: propensity (which defence the model chooses, compared with humans)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (persona-grounded vs generic system prompt)
map.Models tested: Gemini 2.5, Gemini 3.0 Pro, GPT 4.1 mini, GPT 5.1, Grok 4.1 reasoning; human

nodes.label: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
nodes.question:
Can a text version of Among Us elicit open-ended, goal-directed deception (the model works out
for itself that it should deceive, given only the rules), and can it measure deception and
detection as separate, unbounded capabilities? Do activation probes and SAE features trained on
simple honesty datasets detect this deception out of distribution? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Deception vs detection: frontier reasoning models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek-R1, Grok-3) have the highest Deception Elo (≈1,800–1,850 by plot reading) and win rates (≈50–60%); Qwen-2.5-7B and Claude 3 Opus lowest (≈1,580–1,600) (Fig. 2 p. 3). On Detection Elo, small and non-reasoning models are comparable to frontier ones; most reasoning ("RL") models lie above the slope-1 line in deception-vs-detection (Fig. 5 p. 5; §3.3 p. 6). Against release date, deception rises (quadratic fit) and detection does not (Fig. 16 p. 24). No statistical test of the RL vs non-RL difference is given.
Size and role: in 400 Llama-3.3 vs Phi-4 games, Llama-3.3 wins more as impostor, Phi-4 more as crewmate (Fig. 3 p. 4).
Judge labels: GPT-4o-mini scores are poorly calibrated (few scores 3–7) but separate binary labels; crewmates almost never lie, impostors sometimes tell the truth to build trust (Fig. 4 p. 5).

map.Skills measured: deceiving-detecting (impostor deception vs crewmate detection); other: lying/deception detection from activations (probes, SAEs)
map.Scoring: mixed (rule-decided win/loss for Elo; GPT-4o-mini judge only for probe labels)
map.Opponents: LLM
map.Training evaluated: none (probes are trained as detectors; SAE steering tried and fails; no agent training)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (deception vs detection compared observationally across models, not via training)
map.Models tested: 18 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet ± thinking, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, DeepSeek-R1, R1-distill-Llama-70B, DeepSeek-V3, Grok-3-beta, o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro preview, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-235B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Phi-4, Mistral-Small-3.1-24B); probes on Phi-4, SAEs on Llama-3.3-70B

nodes.label: TextArena
nodes.question:
Can a large, extensible collection of competitive text games with a Gym-style interface and a live
TrueSkill leaderboard (models vs models vs humans) give a relative, non-saturating measure of LLM
skills, including social ones (negotiation, ToM, deception), and serve as an RL training source?
(pp. 1–3)
findings: Soft-skill radar (Fig. 1 p. 1): Humanity above claude-3.5-sonnet, qwen-plus and gpt-4o on all 10 skills, but each axis is normalised separately and no numbers are given.

Per-game TrueSkill (Fig. 2 p. 2, "preliminary", read off the bars): Humanity first on DontSayIt (~34) and TicTacToe (~35.5), second on Poker behind claude-3.7-sonnet-thinking, third on Snake, mid-pack on SecretMafia (claude-3.7-sonnet first, ~38); models include o3, o3-mini, claude-3.7-sonnet (± thinking), grok-3-beta, gemini-2.5-pro-preview-03-25, deepseek-chat-v3-0324, gpt-4o-2024-11-20. Caption: results mix game skill with rule/format understanding; some reasoning models reveal their cards or roles.
Positioning (Table 1 p. 5): only framework among 9 compared with all four of Gym API, online evaluation, model-vs-model and model-vs-human.

nodes.label: SocialGym: Evaluating LLM Social Intelligence through Verifiable Multi-Agent Games
nodes.question:
Can a suite of social games with rule-decided outcomes (no LLM judge) measure LLM social
intelligence across many kinds of interaction (cooperation, coordination, negotiation, bluffing,
hidden-role deduction, coalitions) and on every side of a game? Do rankings agree across game
families? And can an inference-time method (a playbook written from self-play) improve play?
(pp. 1–2)
findings: Overall leaderboard (18 competitive games): GPT-5-mini 1122 (win 68.5%), GPT-4o 1066, GPT-4o-mini 1019, Gemma3-27B 1019, Qwen3-32B 1008, Gemma3-12B 997, Gemma3-4B 955, Qwen3-4B 953, Qwen2.5-3B 934, Qwen3-1.7B 922 (Fig. 2, p. 4). 38 of 45 pairs separated at 95% (App. E p. 15).

No model best everywhere: Qwen3-1.7B (last overall) is first on Sheriff, Insider and the Minority Game (p. 5). In Sheriff, Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma3-4B rarely smuggle (2%, 6%) and inspect most bribed bags (84%, 64%) (Table 11, p. 27).

Rankings shift across families — Spearman with the overall ranking: hidden-role 0.96, social strategy 0.85, normal-form 0.55, bluffing 0.47, economic 0.04; between families: hidden-role vs social strategy 0.88, economic vs others 0.02–0.31 (Fig. 4, p. 6; Table 13, p. 28). Split-half reliability: normal-form 0.89, economic 0.68, bluffing 0.90, hidden-role 0.94, social strategy 0.55 — so the normal-form, bluffing and economic reorderings exceed what noise would allow (p. 28). Hidden-role games supply 43% of episodes and alone reproduce the overall ranking (Spearman 0.96, 42 of 45 pairs) (App. E p. 15) — the overall score is largely a hidden-role score.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (Bargaining, Bohnanza trading, Sheriff bribes), cooperating (Stag Hunt, Public Goods, Battle of the Sexes), competing, persuading (Survivor, Dead Last), deceiving-detecting (bluffing and hidden-role games), other: theory of mind, strategic and probabilistic reasoning
map.Scoring: rules (rule-computed game scores → Bradley–Terry Elo; four cooperation games as pairwise win rates)
map.Opponents: LLM (round-robin cross-play, no self-play); a uniformly random player as anchor
map.Training evaluated: prompting (SPaRTan self-play playbooks, training-free); no SFT or RL
map.Transfer between skills measured: yes, prompting only (playbooks written from the other games, (n−1)→1), three games, two models
map.Models tested: GPT-5-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemma3-27B/12B/4B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-1.7B

nodes.label: From Passive Delegates to Strategic Negotiators: Reinforcing Social Reasoning in Small Language Models with SocialRL
nodes.question:
Can a small model (4B) be post-trained to act as a strategic *delegate* — protect its principal's
private information, anchor, concede selectively, walk away — instead of the friendly, agreeable,
leaky behaviour of assistant models? Does training in one negotiation/coordination domain transfer
to the others, and can the per-domain specialists be merged into one model? Does explicit
theory-of-mind supervision help? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Specialists reach GPT range (Table 2, p. 11): base 4B avg 0.389 → domain-trained 0.619 (DnD 0.656, CaSiNo 0.503, Craigslist 0.583, Job 0.594, Calendar 0.540, Marketplace 0.838) vs GPT-4.1 0.625, GPT-5.1 0.619, GPT-5.2 0.613. GPT-5.5 is clearly better at 0.708 (Craigslist 0.746, Marketplace 0.985). Calendar specialist (0.540) is below all GPTs (0.573–0.702).

Transfer matrix (Table 3, p. 12; deltas vs base computed from the table): strongest is the price pair, Craigslist→Marketplace +0.317 and Marketplace→Craigslist +0.184. Calendar is a destructive donor (Craigslist −0.151, Job −0.168; out-transfer −0.060). Job Interview is the broad donor (+0.026). Full matrix in the overlap section below.

Cascade order matters (Table 5, p. 14): transfer-aware 0.627 ± 0.004 vs random 0.578 ± 0.008 (text says 0.584) vs anti-transfer 0.562 ± 0.010. Calendar ends at 0.742, above its own specialist (0.540), and rises *after* CaSiNo/DnD stages with no Calendar updates (0.621 → 0.733 → 0.758, Table 4, p. 14). Craigslist dips during allocation stages (0.614 → 0.489) then recovers.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (allocation, price, multi-issue contract, preference-conflict scheduling); keeping secrets only as a side measure (leakage rates); other: theory of mind (preference inference, next-action prediction)
map.Scoring: rules (normalised utility); behaviour rates by unstated method
map.Opponents: LLM (3 unnamed fixed opponents; not specified)
map.Tests: capability (propensity changes — leakage, fabrication — reported anecdotally)
map.Training evaluated: prompting / SFT / RL (PPO, cascade RL, on-policy distillation); no multi-agent

map.Models tested: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (trained); GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.5 (baselines); GPT-5.2 as ToM teacher

nodes.label: How Far Are We on the Decision-Making of LLMs? Evaluating LLMs' Gaming Ability in Multi-Agent Environments
nodes.question:
How good are LLMs at decisions in multi-player, multi-round classic games? How robust is
performance to sampling, temperature and prompt wording? Do CoT or persona prompts help? Do models
generalize when game parameters change, i.e. beyond memorized textbook settings? (pp. 1–3, 8)
findings: Leaderboard (Overall, mean ± sd over 5 runs): Gemini-1.5-Pro 69.8±1.6, GPT-4o 66.7±4.7, LLaMA-3.1-70B 65.9±3.3, GPT-4-turbo 62.4±2.7, Mixtral-8x22B 62.4±2.2, LLaMA-3.1-405B 61.8±4.7, Qwen-2-72B 56.7±3.4, LLaMA-3.1-8B 56.0±3.1, Gemini-1.0-Pro 45.7±3.4, GPT-3.5 1106/0125/0613 45.1/44.4/42.7, Mixtral-8x7B 43.4±2.2 (Table 1 p. 2). LLaMA-3.1-405B scores below the 70B model because it stays home in El Farol (20.5 vs 59.7) (p. 10).

Per-game profiles disagree strongly: GPT-4-turbo gets 98.1 on Divide the Dollar but 0.9 on Diner's Dilemma and 23.0 on El Farol. Mixtral-8x7B gets 1.2 on Divide the Dollar but 76.4 on Diner's Dilemma. GPT-3.5-0613 is *best* on Diner's Dilemma among the closed models (67.0) (Table 1 p. 2). The Overall score hides near-opposite profiles.

GPT-3.5 (0125) behaviour (Overall 45.9 in the default run, p. 5): it starts at ~50 in Guess 2/3 and then moves down (65.4). It cooperates spontaneously without communication: it contributes to the public pot despite a −80% return (41.2), and mostly orders the cheap dish in Diner's Dilemma, so it scores 4.0 there (p. 6). It rarely targets the strongest shooter (20.0) and never misses on purpose (p. 7). It proposes non-optimal pirate splits and votes wrongly (80.6) (pp. 7–8). Its decisions follow the last round's outcome more than equilibrium reasoning (p. 5).

map.Skills measured: cooperating (Guess 2/3, El Farol, Divide the Dollar), competing (Public Goods, Diner's Dilemma and Sealed-Bid Auction scored for self-interest; Battle Royale), negotiating value (Pirate Game propose/vote, no talk), other (equilibrium / K-level reasoning, mixed strategies)
map.Scoring: rules (distance to NE / optimal action, rescaled 0–100)
map.Opponents: LLM (9 copies of the same model); scripted fixed-strategy co-players in App. G
map.What about the model it tests: both (scored as capability, but Betraying-game scores largely reflect propensity to cooperate or defect)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (CoT, personas, prompt paraphrases, temperature; CipherChat jailbreak)

nodes.label: AI safety via debate
nodes.question:
Can a zero-sum debate between two agents, judged by a human, supervise AI systems on questions too
hard for the human to judge directly? (abstract, pp. 1–2)
findings: MNIST (Table 2, p. 8; p. 10): judge accuracy from random pixels 59.4% (6 px) and 48.2% (4 px); honest-player win rate with precommitted lies 88.9% (6 px) and 85.2% (4 px); without precommit 74.4% and 59.7%. Precommit is "crucial" (p. 10). Without averaging over 3 seeds, 87.7% / 83.8%.
Successful lies concentrate on claiming 8 or 9 (e.g. 5 → 8, 4 → 9), likely because only nonzero pixels can be revealed (Fig. 3, p. 9). The game has a second-mover advantage (p. 9).
Informal human play: "extremely difficult to lie" when players know the game (p. 11); no numbers.

map.Skills measured: not a benchmark (the method is a persuade-the-judge game; the experiment
map.Scoring: not a benchmark (judge decides; a CNN classifier in the experiment, humans proposed).
map.Opponents: not a benchmark (MCTS agents in MNIST; humans informally).
map.Training evaluated: none (MCTS planning; self-play RL proposed only).
map.Models tested: none (no LLMs; MNIST CNN judge + MCTS debaters).

nodes.label: One Model, All Roles: Multi-Turn, Multi-Agent Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Conversational Social Intelligence
nodes.question:
Can one LLM learn conversational social intelligence (goal pursuit, empathy, persuasion,
compromise) by role-playing *every* participant of a multi-turn, multi-party conversation and being
trained with RL on end-of-episode rewards, with no human supervision of behaviour? Does training
on competitive goals also produce collaborative behaviour? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Trained SOTOPIA metrics, small gains (normalized scores, trained / SOTOPIA-RL / base; Fig. 3 top, p. 7): believability 0.712 / 0.696 / 0.651; goal 0.666 / 0.656 / 0.601; knowledge 0.623 / 0.610 / 0.574; relationship 0.223 / 0.209 / 0.219; social rules −0.017 / −0.035 / −0.020; average 0.309 / 0.291 / 0.299. Secret and financial benefit omitted (all near zero). Note SOTOPIA-RL's average is *below* base, and relationship barely moves.

Untrained ("emergent") judge metrics (Fig. 3 bottom, p. 7): mutual benefit seeking 0.771 / 0.755 / 0.730; compromise seeking 0.737 / 0.727 / 0.668; empathy 0.687 / 0.684 / 0.677; strategic commitment 0.696 / 0.682 / 0.684; persuasion 0.573 / 0.555 / 0.555; average 0.695 / 0.681 / 0.663. The text calls these "substantially larger" gains (p. 7); vs base the average gap is +0.032 (vs +0.010 on trained metrics), but vs SOTOPIA-RL it is only +0.014, and compromise seeking's big jump is mostly shared with SOTOPIA-RL (+0.059 vs +0.069 for OMAR).

"Competition elicits collaboration" (SOTOPIA): the claim rests on the rises in mutual-benefit and compromise seeking above, plus qualitative examples (Fig. 4, p. 8; text pp. 7–8). The authors themselves explain it as the agent seeking partial goal fulfilment "where the LLM-as-a-judge would give higher partial scores" (p. 8), i.e. the judge rewards compromise.

nodes.label: When Agents Persuade: Rhetoric Generation and Mitigation in LLMs
nodes.venue: ICLR 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild (arXiv v2, 1 Apr 2026)
nodes.question:
Can LLMs write propaganda when asked, which rhetorical techniques do they use compared with
human propagandists, and how well do SFT, DPO and ORPO suppress it? (RQ1–RQ3, pp. 1–2)
findings: Compliance: the detector labels 99% of GPT-4o, 77% of Llama-3.1 and 99% of Mistral 3 propaganda-prompt outputs as propaganda (p. 6). GPT-4, o1, o3 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet refused the same prompt (pp. 9–10).

Techniques vs humans: all three models use loaded language, exaggeration/minimization and flag-waving more than human propaganda; GPT-4o flag-waving ≈3× and appeal to fear ≈4× human rates; Llama uses name-calling ≈3× less (p. 7, Table 8 p. 19). GPT-4o uses every technique significantly more than the other two (p. 7).
Prompt guardrail fails: with the "factual assistant, no propaganda" system prompt, 99% of GPT-4o outputs are still propaganda, ≈ baseline (p. 5).

nodes.label: MAGPIE: A benchmark for Multi-AGent contextual PrIvacy Evaluation
nodes.question:
In multi-party negotiations where private information matters for solving the task, do LLM agents
keep their principal's secrets, still reach agreement, and what strategic behaviours do they show?
(pp. 1–2)
findings: Leakage is high and instructions barely help (Table 1, p. 6): total leakage implicit / explicit — GPT-5 35.1 / 25.0%, Claude-4.1-Opus 35.7 / 31.6%, Llama-4-Maverick 39.5 / 32.5%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 56.0 / 50.7%, GPT-4 61.4 / 56.0%. Explicit instructions cut leakage by only 4–10 points (p. 6). Most leakage is partial (hints), e.g. GPT-4 implicit 48.8% partial vs 12.6% full.
Timing: GPT-4, Gemini and Claude leak much of it by round 2–3; GPT-5 and Llama leak later (Fig. 3a, p. 6–7).
Agreement is rare: consensus implicit GPT-4 13.5%, Gemini 7.9%, GPT-5 5.3%; Claude-4.1-Opus and Llama-4-Maverick 0% in both conditions (p. 7).

map.Skills measured: keeping secrets (contextual privacy), negotiating value, cooperating (reaching consensus), other: behaviour tags (manipulation, sycophancy, lying, threatening, compromise)
map.Scoring: LLM judge (GPT-5 judges leakage, task completion and behaviour tags)
map.Opponents: LLM (co-agents)
map.Tests: both (task completion; leakage and behaviour when privacy is implicit)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-4.1-Opus, GPT-4, Llama-4-Maverick

nodes.label: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
nodes.question:
Do language models know what they know? Three steps: are their probabilities calibrated on
multiple-choice questions; can they judge whether their *own* sampled answers are correct
(P(True)); and can they be trained to predict, before answering, whether they will get a question
right (P(IK)), and does that carry over to new tasks? (§1)
findings: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice when they see the options, and calibration improves with size and with few-shot prompting (Figs. 4–6, §2). No clear link between accuracy and calibration within BIG-Bench (Fig. 5).
"None of the above" breaks it: replacing an option sharply lowers accuracy and calibration; even the 52B model avoids using it, also at 20-shot (Fig. 7, §3.1).
RLHF policies look badly miscalibrated, but one temperature (T = 2.5) largely fixes it on three evaluations (Fig. 9, §3.3).

nodes.label: Why Language Models Hallucinate
nodes.question:
Why do language models state confident falsehoods instead of saying "I don't know", and why
doesn't post-training remove this? (§1)
findings: Pretraining makes some errors unavoidable: generative error rate ≳ 2 × the misclassification rate of "is it valid?" (§1.1). For arbitrary facts with no pattern (e.g. birthdays), the hallucination rate after pretraining is at least the share of facts that appear once in training ("singleton rate") (§3.3).

Calibration and errors go together: cross-entropy pretraining yields calibrated base models, and a calibrated model must make errors; a model that never errs (always "I don't know") would be uncalibrated (§3.1). GPT-4's calibration on multiple choice is good before RL and worse after (Fig. 2, reprinted from the GPT-4 report).

Evaluations reward guessing: under 0–1 grading, abstaining is never optimal for any belief about the answer (Observation 1, §4.1). Most leading benchmarks give no credit for "I don't know" (Table 2), so a model that always guesses beats an honest one; models stay in "test-taking mode" (§1.2, §4).

nodes.label: CooperBench: Why Coding Agents Cannot be Your Teammates Yet
nodes.question:
Can two coding agents, each given its own feature on the same repository, coordinate by chat
well enough that their merged patches pass both features' tests? Does the chat help, and how do
they fail?
findings: Curse of coordination: two agents do worse than one doing both features. GPT-5 0.48 Solo vs 0.28 Coop; Claude 0.47 vs 0.26; MiniMax 0.36 vs 0.14; Qwen Coder 0.22 vs 0.13 (bar labels in Fig. 4, p. 7; the text rounds the leaders to "only 25%", p. 3). Pooled retention (Coop AUC / Solo AUC) is 0.59; MiniMax retains only 0.46, while the weakest coder (Qwen Instruct) retains the most, 0.68: coding skill does not predict coordination (pp. 24–25).
The gap is largest on mid-difficulty tasks (p. 7–8).
More agents is worse: 68.6% with 2, 46.5% with 3, 30.0% with 4 agents (46 tasks, p. 8).

map.Skills measured: cooperating (two agents implementing overlapping features in one codebase, coordinating by chat), other: software engineering
map.Scoring: rules (merge the two patches, run both test sets); GPT-5 judge only for the failure taxonomy
map.Opponents: LLM (partner is the same model)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, MiniMax-M2, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct

nodes.label: Scalable Evaluation of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Melting Pot
nodes.question:
How can multi-agent RL be evaluated on generalisation to unfamiliar co-players, the way
supervised learning is evaluated on held-out test data, without hand-building each test
environment? The answer proposed: use pre-trained agents as the test set (pp. 1–2).
findings: Overall (p. 8): V-MPO best on average, then OPRE, then A3C; similar on mixed-motive games, V-MPO ahead on competitive ones such as King of the Hill (SC 1: V-MPO 627.8 vs −895 to −990 for the others and −991.1 for the exploiter; p. 28).

Training score does not predict test score: prosocial OPRE and A3C reach about the same self-play score as their selfish versions in Bach or Stravinsky (A3C 10.8 vs 10.2) but collapse when visiting a population of Bach fans (8.3 vs 1.9) (p. 9; p. 27); in Stag Hunt SC 1 A3C scores 28.6 vs 6.6 for prosocial A3C (p. 29). They learned only cooperation in self-play and are exploitable by defectors at test time (p. 9).

Maximising collective reward often makes policies less robust than maximising individual reward (p. 2); prosocial agents underperform overall (p. 9) — but in Clean Up only the prosocial agents learn anything (self-play: 0.0 for all selfish agents vs 36.9 / 72.8 / 188.6 prosocial; visiting altruists SC 0: A3C 91.5 vs prosocial A3C 380.3, random 69.1; p. 27). The paper's conclusion: agents must "contingently balance selfishness and prosociality" (p. 9).

map.Skills measured: cooperating, competing, deceiving-detecting (feinting in Running with Scissors,
map.Scoring: rules (environment reward, focal per-capita return).
map.Opponents: learned agents (pre-trained RL bots, some with a scripted high-level controller).
map.Training evaluated: multi-agent (MARL: A3C, V-MPO, OPRE, each selfish vs prosocial reward).
map.Transfer measured: yes, to unseen co-players within a substrate; no transfer between substrates
map.Models tested: A3C, V-MPO, OPRE (+ prosocial variants), plus exploiter and random baselines.

nodes.label: Deal or No Deal? End-to-End Learning for Negotiation Dialogues
nodes.question:
Can one neural model learn to negotiate in free natural language end to end, with no annotated
dialogue states, by imitating human dialogues? And does it negotiate better if it is trained
(RL) or decodes (rollout planning) to maximise its own reward instead of likelihood? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Against the LIKELIHOOD model (Table 1, p. 7): score (all) LIKELIHOOD 5.4 vs 5.5, RL 7.1 vs 4.2, ROLLOUTS 7.3 vs 5.1, RL + ROLLOUTS 8.3 vs 4.2; agreement 87.9 → 94.4%; Pareto-optimal deals 49.6 → 74.8%.

Against humans (Table 1, p. 7): score (all) LIKELIHOOD 4.7 vs 5.8, RL 4.3 vs 5.0, ROLLOUTS 5.2 vs 5.4, RL + ROLLOUTS 4.6 vs 4.2. Agreement falls from 76.5% (LIKELIHOOD) to 67.3% (RL) and 57.2% (RL + ROLLOUTS); score on agreed deals rises from 6.2 to 8.0; Pareto-optimal deals rise from 66.2 to 82.4%. RL + ROLLOUTS is the only system that beats its human partner on score (all).

So the claim that RL agents "outperform their supervised counterparts in negotiations with humans" (p. 1) holds on agreed deals only (6.4 vs 6.2): on score (all), RL alone scores *less* than LIKELIHOOD (4.3 vs 4.7), and so does RL + ROLLOUTS (4.6). The best absolute score against humans is ROLLOUTS (5.2) (Table 1, p. 7). The paper says "significantly" but reports no test, no confidence intervals and no number of human dialogues per system.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (deceiving appears only as anecdotes).
map.Scoring: rules (points from the private value functions, agreement check), plus perplexity for
map.Opponents: learned agents (the fixed supervised LIKELIHOOD model) and human (MTurk).
map.Training evaluated: SFT (supervised imitation) and RL (REINFORCE against a fixed partner), plus
map.Transfer measured: no (only held-out scenarios of the same task).
map.Models tested: GRU seq2seq models trained from scratch (LIKELIHOOD, RL, ROLLOUTS, RL + ROLLOUTS).

nodes.label: Whose Side Is Your Agent On? Multi-Party Principal Loyalty in LLM Agents
nodes.question:
When an agent acts for a principal while talking to a counterparty whose interests conflict,
how often does it betray the principal (leak, capitulate, signal weakness), and can prompting or
distillation fix that without making it over-refuse? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Split: nine models at ≤ 19.5% harm ("selective": Gemini-2.5-flash 5.5%, Claude Opus 18.1%, Claude Sonnet 19.5%), three at ≥ 53.6% ("over-refusing": GPT-5-mini 53.6%, GPT-5 71.1%, Qwen3.5-27B 75.3%), GLM-4.6 46.0% (Fig. 3, p. 7). Over-refusers fail almost entirely by refusing the principal's legitimate asks (MI 67–82%) (Table 2, p. 8). On held-out items GPT-5 reaches 93%.

Prompt scaffold holds the selective cluster ≤ 20% (Claude Sonnet 19.4%) but doesn't help, even harms, over-refusers (p = 0.0002) (p. 9). It creates new over-refusal of the principal (9/12), which the reader tag cuts to 3/12 (pp. 9–10).

Distillation: per-token KL is the only variant significantly better than the base (harm 47.8 → 39.2 per 108, p = 0.011), but only under the primary judge; under the second judge p = 0.75 (pp. 11, 15). ≈10-point train-to-held-out gap (p. 13).

map.Scoring: mixed (deterministic leak probe plus two LLM judges)
map.Opponents: LLM (counterparty personas)
map.Tests: propensity (whether the agent leaks or gives in when not told to)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (loyalty scaffold) / SFT (per-turn SFT, DPO, per-token KL distillation) / RL (DAPO)
