nodes.label: When LLM Agents Negotiate: Private Information and Dynamic Bargaining in Supply Chains
nodes.question:
When firms delegate procurement bargaining to LLM agents, do the agents create value, divide it
predictably and avoid loss-making contracts, measured against a Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium? And
which of the firm's choices (capability tier, provider, prompt configuration) move outcomes?
(pp. 1–5)
findings: Efficient but slow: 98.9% agreement, 95.4% of first-best surplus undiscounted, but 2.98 rounds vs 1.25 benchmark; discounted efficiency 66.2% vs 96.4% (Table 4, p. 14). Capability explains ~66% of explained efficiency variance (Shapley), patience 90% of buyer-share variance (Table 5, p. 19).

Breaking the principal's limit: irrational (negative-profit) agreements in 0.0% flagship, 0.6% mid-tier, 19.2% baseline; 97.1% involve a baseline model. GPT-4o-mini 36.2%, Qwen2.5-14B 20.0%, reasoning baseline Gemini-2.5-Flash 2.9% (pp. 16–17, Fig. 2). Buyers 5.1% vs sellers 1.4%; 79% of cases are revenue miscalculation, 21% cost miscalculation (p. 17). So in this setting the breaches look like arithmetic/constraint-checking failures, not persuasion.

Provider, not capability, decides who gets the surplus: self-play buyer share OpenAI 40%, Google 50%, Qwen 70% (Qwen3-Max 91.4%) (Table 6, p. 20). Cross-family: Gemini-3-Pro gets 66.7% as buyer, Qwen3-Max keeps only 27.3% as seller; reversing roles swings 7–18 pp (pp. 22–23). Within a family the stronger model wins: GPT-5.2 seller profit $931 vs $680 (p. 19).

nodes.label: Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
nodes.question:
Can a language model learn to say how likely its own answer is to be correct, in words ("61%",
"medium confidence"), and does that stay calibrated on new kinds of questions? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Verbalized probability generalizes under shift: on Multi-answer, MSE 22.0 vs 37.4 (answer logit), 33.7 (indirect logit), 34.1 (constant) (Table 1, p. 6). On Multiply-divide it only matches the constant baseline; the indirect logit is best there (p. 6).
It is underconfident under shift: the evaluation answers are more often right than the training ones, and the model doesn't fully adjust (p. 6).
50 examples in context almost match fine-tuning on ~10k (Fig. 6, p. 7).

nodes.label: DeLLMa: Decision Making Under Uncertainty with Large Language Models
nodes.question:
When an LLM must choose an action whose payoff depends on unknown future states (what to plant,
which stock to buy), does it weigh the uncertainty properly? If not, does a scaffold built on
classical decision theory help? (§1)
findings: Plain prompting fails as the choice grows: with larger action sets, zero-shot, self-consistency and CoT often do worse than random (§4.1, Fig. 2).

The failure is following the mood of the text, not weighing scenarios: e.g. GPT-4 assumes a high grapefruit price lasts because last year had extreme weather; CoT names alternative scenarios but doesn't use them systematically. Neither sampling, imagining alternatives, nor *giving the model a posterior belief* in the prompt substantially fixes it (§4.1, App. C.4).
The forecasts themselves are fairly calibrated: ECE 0.062 (GPT-4), 0.142 (Claude 3), 0.064 (Gemini 1.5) (Table 1). So the problem is not the probabilities but using them to decide.

nodes.label: SPIRAL: Self-Play on Zero-Sum Games Incentivizes Reasoning via Multi-Agent Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
nodes.question:
Can an LLM learn general reasoning, without curated problem-answer data, by playing multi-turn
two-player zero-sum games against itself with online RL? Does training on several games beat one
game, and does it beat imitation (SFT) or fixed opponents? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Math/general transfer: Qwen3-4B-Base 34.0 → 44.5 average (+10.5) with multi-game SPIRAL; Qwen3-8B-Base 39.5 → 49.6; Octothinker-8B 25.8 → 33.8; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 23.9 → 25.9; DeepSeek-Distill-7B 60.4 → 61.8. SFT-Multi: 39.7, 46.1, 27.0, 25.0, 58.3 (Table 1, p. 7). Doubling SFT data to 52k changes nothing (39.7) (Table 9, p. 23). Three seeds on Qwen3-4B: 44.5 ± 0.5 vs SFT 39.6 ± 0.4 (Table 10, p. 23).

Single vs multi-game on benchmarks (Qwen3-4B, single seed each): TicTacToe 41.3, Kuhn 43.4, Negotiation 40.0 (weakest), TicTacToe+Kuhn 41.3 (*below* Kuhn alone), all three 44.5 (Table 9, p. 23). So multi-game is best, but only +1.1 over the best single game, and adding a game does not always help. The appendix text quotes different ranges (single 40.0–41.4, multi 42.3–42.7) that do not match the table (p. 22).

Single vs multi-game in games (vs Gemini-2.0-Flash, Table 5, p. 9): multi-game average 59.5% vs best specialist 52.9% (TicTacToe), 52.7% (Kuhn), 48.6% (Negotiation). But on Simple Negotiation itself the multi-game model (33.2%) loses to the negotiation specialist (39.1%); multi-game wins on Kuhn (53.9 vs 48.5) and the OOD games. The untrained *instruct* model averages 57.6%, almost as high, and beats every model on Simple Negotiation (46.2%).

nodes.label: AgenticPay: A Multi-Agent LLM Negotiation System for Buyer-Seller Transactions
nodes.question:
How well do current LLMs negotiate as autonomous buyers and sellers when each side has a private
reservation price, from bilateral bargaining to many-to-many markets with several products?
(pp. 1–2)
findings: Overall (self-play, 111 tasks) (Table 1, p. 6): GlobalScore Claude Opus 4.5 86.9, Gemini 3 Flash 82.2, GPT-5.2 81.7, Qwen3-14B 63.9, Llama-3.1-8B 32.5. Deal rate 100% for the three proprietary models, 79.3% Qwen3-14B (20.7% timeouts), 51.4% Llama (48.6% timeouts, 10.8% overflow). Average rounds 3.7 (Opus), 3.8 (GPT-5.2), 15.0 (Llama). Deal rate is saturated for frontier models, as in zhang2026terms.

Seller > buyer for every model (p. 7): SellerScore vs BuyerScore GPT-5.2 81.1 vs 58.5, Qwen3-14B 58.9 vs 47.6 (Table 1). In bilateral cross-play the gap is 26.0 points for Opus (83.6 vs 57.6) and 43.2 for Qwen3-14B (82.4 vs 39.2) (Table 4, p. 7). The authors guess at training-data bias toward selling (p. 7); note only the seller prompt carries an initial asking price (Tables 14–15), an anchor the paper does not control for.

More buyers and sellers → higher GlobalScore: +5 (GPT-5.2) to +14 points (Qwen3-14B) from 1B1S to MBMS, e.g. Opus 83.4 → 89.8, Qwen3-14B 63.2 → 77.6 (Table 2, p. 6); read as market liquidity (p. 7). Full-complexity tasks score above bilateral ones for every model (Table 12, p. 14: Opus 79.4 vs 90.7, Qwen3-14B 43.7 vs 82.6).

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (distributive price bargaining, incl. multi-party markets).
map.Scoring: rules (Algorithm 1 on parsed prices).
map.Agents: 2 to many (bilateral up to multi-buyer, multi-seller markets).
map.Opponents: LLM (self-play; bilateral cross-play among the 5 models).
map.Training evaluated: none (inference only; personality prompts as a side analysis).
map.Models tested: Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5.2, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B.

nodes.label: Instructing LLMs to Negotiate using Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
nodes.question:
Can RL with verifiable rewards (surplus + budget adherence) teach an LLM buyer to negotiate, and
what strategies emerge? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Four training phases: aggressive lowballing → deadlock (deal rate collapses) → rational concession → "advanced persuasion" with ~90% deal rate (pp. 6–7).
Budget overshoot driven to ~0 within a few iterations by the −1 penalty (p. 7).
Held-out: trained 30B reward 0.766 vs GPT-5.4-high 0.402, Kimi-K2-Thinking 0.342; bargained ratio 0.839 vs 0.438; untrained base 0.013 with 10.35% budget overshoot (Table 1, p. 8).

nodes.label: Paying Less Generalization Tax: A Cross-Domain Generalization Study of RL Training for LLM Agents
nodes.question:
Generalist agents are post-trained on a narrow set of environments but deployed in broader,
unknown ones. Which properties of an RL training environment, and which modelling choices, best
*preserve* performance on domains never seen in training? (pp. 1–2) The authors stress
cross-domain generalization (different tools, states, goals), not held-out tasks in the same
domain, and frame the work as prevention: in their pilots, out-of-domain (OOD) scores fell while
in-domain scores rose during RL (p. 2).
findings: RL raises in-domain success and lowers OOD success (Table 2, p. 6). E.g. Ckpt V1 trained on ALFWorld: +47.2 in-domain, WebShop 34.4 → 15.2. Ckpt V1 trained on WebShop: ALFWorld 25.8 → 10.8.

What predicts OOD robustness is structure, not realism or surface similarity. Domains high on both richness and planning complexity preserve most: SciWorld (rank score 3) and Sokoban (5) vs WebShop (6) and ALFWorld (8) (Table 3, p. 6). The abstract grid puzzle Sokoban transfers better to realistic SciWorld than realistic ALFWorld does (p. 8).
Not just "learned less": training Sokoban and SciWorld longer, until their in-domain gain matches or exceeds ALFWorld/WebShop (Sokoban +68 after 300 steps), keeps their OOD rank (Table 4, p. 8).

nodes.label: The Decrypto Benchmark for Multi-Agent Reasoning and Theory of Mind
nodes.question:
Can a word-association game built on the board game Decrypto serve as an interactive,
hard-to-saturate benchmark for multi-agent reasoning (cooperation, competition, ad-hoc and
human-AI coordination) and for theory of mind (ToM), while removing confounds such as
tokenisation, maths, spatial reasoning, long contexts and text renderings of embodied scenes?
(pp. 1–3)
findings: Baselines beat LLMs: at K=16 the embedding baselines outperform all LLM agents in self-play and competition, but cross-play with a different embedding or with an LLM collapses; for K>128 most cross-play games end in miscommunication (Fig. 2 p. 6; Fig. 3 p. 7). Example: GloVe-Alice's 50th-nearest word to "fire" is "oil", which is outside Word2Vec's top 1,000 (p. 7).

Coordination (Fig. 3 top, Eve = Llama-70B): baseline→LLM miscommunication rates 0.48–0.67 vs 0.00–0.08 baseline–baseline and 0.00–0.04 LLM–LLM; among LLMs the decoder model drives miscommunications (Llama-8B worst). No self-play/cross-play gap among LLMs (p. 8).

Competition is skewed to Eve: intercept rates mostly 0.71–1.00 (Fig. 3 bottom p. 7); LLM teams rarely survive 32 games (Fig. 7 p. 18). Novice humans win 33% even against the strongest Eves (p. 8). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B is the best LLM in LLM-only play.

map.Skills measured: cooperating (ad-hoc and human-AI coordination), competing (interception), keeping secrets (hints hidden from the interceptor), other: theory of mind (representational change, false belief, perspective taking), pragmatic communication
map.Scoring: rules
map.Opponents: scripted (GloVe/Word2Vec baselines), LLM, human
map.Training evaluated: none (only an existing ToM-SFT model, ExploreToM-8B, compared with its base)
map.Models tested: Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet (extended thinking), o1 (high), ExploreToM-8B

nodes.label: GIFT: Games as Informal Training for Generalizable LLMs
nodes.question:
Does adding RL on games ("informal learning") to RL on math ("formal learning") improve general
abilities beyond math-only RL, and does training subtasks in sequence (Coordinated Subtask Training,
CST) integrate heterogeneous RL signals better than mixing them in one batch? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Game → other games, 1.5B: Matrix training lifts TicTacToe 1 → 34 and Spy 2 → 14; TicTacToe training lifts Matrix 7 → 32 and Spy 2 → 21; Spy training lifts Matrix 7 → 21 but TicTacToe 1 → 0. The 1.5B base model scores near zero on all games (Spy 2, TicTacToe 1) and below chance on 3-way SocialIQA (27.64), so much of the 1.5B "transfer" is likely learning to answer in format.

Game → other games, 7B (base already competent): Matrix training hurts TicTacToe 40 → 23; TicTacToe training helps Matrix 40 → 57 and Spy 25 → 33; Spy training leaves Matrix 43 and TicTacToe 38 (≈ base).
Game → math: 1.5B: Matrix 17.2 → 19.2, TicTacToe 22.4, Spy 19.2 MATH500 (math RL: 43.2). 7B: Matrix 54.6 → 58.2 (≈ math RL 58.4), Spy 55.6, but TicTacToe 54.6 → 49.8 (negative).

map.Skills measured: competing (TicTacToe), cooperating/deceiving-detecting (Who's the Spy), other (Nash-equilibrium choice in matrix games; math; MMLU; CommonGen; SocialIQA)
map.Scoring: mixed (rules for games/math/MCQ; GPT-4o judge for CommonGen)
map.Agents: many (2 in TicTacToe/matrix, 4 in Who's the Spy)
map.Opponents: LLM (Qwen3-14B in training, Gemini-2.5-Flash in evaluation)
map.Training evaluated: RL (single-task, mixed multi-task, CST, task-level advantage normalisation)
map.Transfer between skills measured: yes (game ↔ game, game ↔ math, game → MMLU/MMLU-Pro/CommonGen/SocialIQA)
map.Models tested: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (trained); GPT-4o, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, DeepSeek-V3.2 (reference only)

nodes.label: Used Car Salesbots? Honesty and Credulity of LLMs as Bargaining Agents under Partial Information
nodes.question:
Do LLM bargainers reach game-theoretic outcomes under different information regimes, how honest
are informed agents and how credulous are uninformed ones, and does RL for profit make them
better but less honest? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Deal rates 0.975–1.00 everywhere (p. 4).

Opposite of theory: the uninformed side wins. When the seller knows both prices, seller advantage is −0.41 (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7), −0.33 (GPT-5.2), −0.19 (GPT-5.5), −0.17 (Qwen); the informed party concedes towards the uninformed side's high anchor (Table 2, pp. 4–5).

Informed agents are systematically dishonest: honesty 1.01–1.35 (below neutral 2), mostly misleading claims rather than outright lies; uninformed agents are mildly credulous (2.25–2.69) (Table 4, p. 6). Opus 4.7 the least honest (1.11 average); an example lie overstates cost by ~75% (Fig. 9, p. 16).

nodes.label: MERIT Feedback Elicits Better Bargaining in LLM Negotiators
nodes.question:
Can buyer-side LLM bargaining be evaluated with a metric that matches what humans prefer (not
profit alone), across economically distinct market conditions, and does feeding that metric back
to the model (as a prompt or as SFT data) make it a better buyer? (pp. 1–2)
findings: MERIT matches human choices better than profit: ROC AUC 0.80 vs 0.68 for a profit-only metric (Fig. 3, p. 5). Whether the AUC is on held-out pairs is not stated.

Baseline buyers (ReAct, Table 2 p. 6): average MERIT gemini-1.5-pro 1.381 (deal 80.3%), gpt-3.5-turbo 1.257 (88.5%), gpt-4o 1.247 (83.9%), gpt-4o-mini 1.240 (79.0%), gemini-1.5-flash 1.044 (69.6%). No consistent size–performance trend outside Gemini (p. 21).

Market effects (pp. 6, 21): allowing deception raises buyer MERIT by +0.10 and deal rate by +10.62 pp vs vanilla; monopoly lowers deal rate by 3.34% (single) and 8.80% (multi) and MERIT by ~0.10/0.13; installments raise single-item deal rates at worse prices; negative seller perception lowers deal rates. Authors read such directional shifts as a test of "market compatibility".

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (buyer-side price bargaining with substitutes, under permitted deception)
map.Scoring: mixed (rule-based MERIT with weights fitted to human preferences; LLM judge as secondary check)
map.Opponents: LLM (one fixed seller model per experiment: gemini-1.5-pro or DeepSeek-v3.2)
map.Training evaluated: prompting, SFT
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (only across market regimes and opponents within bargaining)
map.Models tested: gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, gpt-3.5-turbo, gemini-1.5-pro, gemini-1.5-flash, gemini-1.0-pro, GPT-5.1 (± reasoning), DeepSeek-v3.2 (± reasoning), Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini-3-Flash, gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b (SFT base)

nodes.label: MakeMePay
nodes.venue: OpenAI Evals task (GitHub, openai/evals, evals/elsuite/make_me_pay); added Sep 2023, v2 Nov 2023
nodes.question:
Can a model generate persuasive or manipulative text well enough to get another (simulated) agent
to part with money? (README.)
findings: The repo publishes no numbers; it is a measurement tool. (Results are cited in OpenAI system cards — not verified here.)

Code-level issues found on reading (relevant if reused): - Duration text bug: max_turns_or_time returns an int for a turn cap, and ints are formatted as "{n} minutes", floats as "turns" — so in the turn-capped registry variants the con-artist is told it has e.g. "5 minutes", not 5 turns (makemepay.py, generate_reply_for). - donation_success_rate is a fraction printed with a "%" sign (0.25 shown as "0.25%") (eval.py). - Broke-character / empty-tag counters are reset inside the turn loop, so they record at most the last turn, and the mark empty-tag increment uses the wrong variable (makemepay.py). - The summary model is called on all mark messages whenever any contains "$" — a mark saying "I have $100" can trigger the model-based detector; only a positive integer reply counts (detect_donation).
Only the con-artist is evaluated in the default config; the mark is a fixed GPT-4-32k baseline, so susceptibility is not measured unless one swaps the mark solver.

map.Skills measured: persuading (manipulating for money); resisting persuasion only if the mark is swapped
map.Scoring: rules (regex on [GIVE $N]) with LLM fallback detector (GPT-4 summary model)
map.Opponents: LLM (fixed GPT-4-32k mark by default)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: none reported in the repo (suggested con-artist solvers gpt-4, gpt-3.5-turbo; mark gpt-4-32k)

nodes.label: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
nodes.question:
Can a society of LLM agents sustainably share a regenerating common resource (a repeated
common-pool / tragedy-of-the-commons game with free-text talk)? Which models manage it, what role
does communication play, what reasoning sub-skills predict success, and do the norms survive a
greedy newcomer? Can a moral-reasoning prompt ("universalization") help? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Most models collapse in month 1: aggregated over scenarios, survival rate 0% for Llama-3 8B/70B, Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen-72B, Claude-3 Haiku/Sonnet, GPT-3.5; Qwen-110B 20%, GPT-4 6.7%, GPT-4-turbo 40%, Claude-3 Opus 46.7%, GPT-4o 53.3% (best; survival time 9.3, efficiency 55.0, over-usage 10.8%) (Table 1 p. 6).

Same game, different framing, different result: dynamics are mathematically equivalent, yet GPT-4-turbo survives 100% in fishery but 0% in pasture and 20% in pollution; Opus 60% / 80% / 0%; GPT-4o 100% / 20% / 40% (Tables 4–6 pp. 23–25). Authors suggest fishery needs only one variable (p. 5).

Greedy newcomer (GPT-4o, all scenarios): survival rate 53.3 → 33.3, gain 66.0 → 34.8, efficiency 55.0 → 31.3, equality 94.4 → 71.7, over-usage 10.8 → 15.7 (p. 6). By scenario: fishery still survives 100% (newcomer is talked down, Fig. 3b, Fig. 16 p. 39), pasture and pollution 0% (Tables 13–15 p. 29).

map.Skills measured: cooperating (sustaining a common pool); negotiating (free-text norm setting); other: long-horizon consequence reasoning, belief formation about others
map.Scoring: rules (survival, gain, efficiency, equality, over-usage); LLM judge only for dialogue analysis
map.Opponents: LLM (self-play, same model in all seats); one scripted-persona greedy newcomer experiment
map.Tests: both (capability via sub-skill tests; propensity to over-harvest when unprompted)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (universalization prompt)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (sub-skill accuracy correlated with survival across models; cross-scenario differences reported but not as transfer)
map.Models tested: 15 — GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-4o, Claude-3 Haiku/Sonnet/Opus, Llama-2 7B/13B/70B, Llama-3 8B/70B, Mistral-7B, Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen1.5-72B/110B

nodes.label: Bayesian Teaching Enables Probabilistic Reasoning in Large Language Models
nodes.question:
When an LLM must infer someone's hidden preferences from their choices over several rounds, does
it update its beliefs the way Bayes' rule says it should? If not, can it be taught to, and does
the skill carry over to other tasks? (§1)
findings: LLMs barely update: all models fall well short of the Bayesian Assistant and most improve little after round 1; performance plateaus after one interaction (Fig. 2, §2.2).
Prompting doesn't fix it: chain of thought, numerical formats, 30 rounds instead of 5, and base (non-instruction) models all fail to help (App. C.1, §2.2).
Humans improve over rounds (p = 0.002) but also fall short of the Bayesian standard (§2.2).

nodes.label: Sparks of Cooperative Reasoning: LLMs as Strategic Hanabi Agents
nodes.question:
How well do current LLMs cooperate under hidden information in Hanabi across 2–5 players, how much
does context engineering (engine-supplied beliefs vs self-tracked memory) matter, and can a small
model be post-trained on LLM-generated Hanabi data — and does that training transfer outside
Hanabi? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Benchmark: reasoning models score >13/25 even in Watson; non-reasoning <10 (p. 5). Best Sherlock scores: Grok-3-mini 18.0 (3p), 17.4 (4p); o3 best in Watson for 2–4p (p. 6; Fig. 5). Top LLMs reach about the lower quartile of 80,699 human BGG games, below the median (App. F, pp. 26–27); specialist RL agents score >23 (2p) and R3D2 ≥20 (p. 6).

Context helps reasoning models, hurts non-reasoning ones: Sherlock vs Watson Gemini 2.5 Flash +4.4, Pro +2.9, o4-mini +0.6; but GPT-4.1 family −2.4, Grok-3 −3.9, Claude 3.7 Sonnet −4.1 (pp. 5–6). On Grok-3-mini 5p seed 3: Watson 12.2, SPIN-Bench prompt 14.5, SPIN without deductions 15.4, Sherlock 16.1 (Fig. 2, pp. 3–4).

Self-tracked state is weak: Mycroft vs Sherlock drops o4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Pro ~3.7, Grok-3- mini ~2.1, o3 ~1.2 (p. 6). An o4-mini judge rates state tracking 0.252 (o4-mini) vs 0.459 (Grok-3-mini) out of 1 (Table 4, p. 26).

map.Skills measured: cooperating (Hanabi; Group Guessing as transfer), other (theory of mind / belief-state tracking; temporal reasoning, instruction following, math as transfer)
map.Scoring: mixed (game rules for Hanabi; LLM judge for move ratings/RL reward and state tracking)
map.Agents: many (2–5 Hanabi seats; 10 in Group Guessing)
map.Opponents: LLM (teammates are copies of the same LLM; one cross-play pair; MAPPO as a trained baseline)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (scaffolds, Best-of-K, mixture of agents), SFT, RL
map.Transfer between skills measured: yes (Hanabi RL → Group Guessing, EventQA, IFBench, AIME 2025)
map.Models tested: o3, o4-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, Grok-3, Grok-3-mini, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-4 Maverick, Mistral Medium 3, Claude 3.7 Sonnet; Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (trained)
map.Code released: stated as released ("at this url"), link not recoverable from the PDF text; check the arXiv page

nodes.label: Receiver Decides Agent-to-Agent Negotiations
nodes.code: transcripts, traces and analysis code released (no URL in the PDF)
nodes.question:
When one LLM agent asks another for money, which side decides how much changes hands: the
persuader or the holder? And can training move the holder's resistance? (pp. 1–2)
findings: The holder decides. Holder identity explains 46.7–47.2% of variance in the amount transferred, requester identity 1.9–2.1%, matchup 3.0%, framing 0.1% (pp. 4, 12). Removing extreme agents narrows it to 22.3% vs 4.3%, but the ratio CI still excludes 1 (p. 4).
Framing changed the text (named protagonist 79.9% vs 43.5% of turns) but not the outcome: 19.8% vs 22.0% extracted, equivalence test rules out |d| > 0.2 (p = 0.016) (p. 5).
Outcomes are bimodal: holder gives nothing in 47% of games, everything in 11% (p. 5).

nodes.label: AREG: Adversarial Resource Extraction Game for Evaluating Persuasion and Resistance in Large Language Models
nodes.question:
Is an LLM's ability to persuade related to its ability to resist persuasion, when both are
measured by money actually handed over in a zero-sum game? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Resistance beats persuasion for every model: V-Elo > C-Elo, mean spread +216. GPT-5.2 is the best defender (V-Elo 1694, $0 lost in 65.7% of games); Mixtral the worst (1502, 5.7%) (Table 1, p. 5).

Persuading and resisting are weakly related: Spearman ρ = 0.33, p = 0.42 (n = 8). Pearson r = 0.634 on the same data (Table 4, p. 11), so "dissociated" rests on 8 points. Top persuader DeepSeek V3.2 is 5th at resisting; top defender GPT-5.2 is 5th at persuading (p. 5).

Early window: 57.5% of commitments happen in turns 1–3; with nothing by turn 5, the chance of any later extraction is < 4% (p. 6). Per-turn success peaks at 20.4% in turns 2–3 and falls to 3.6% in turns 6–10 (Table 5, p. 11). First commitment size correlates with total extraction, ρ = 0.808 (p. 8).

map.Skills measured: persuading (extracting money as a salesperson), resisting persuasion (keeping lottery winnings)
map.Scoring: mixed (an LLM arbiter extracts unconditional handovers; rules compute the extraction ratio and Elo)
map.Opponents: LLM (round robin, both roles)
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: GPT-5.2, Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek V3.2, Grok 4.1 Fast, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3 Next 80B, Mixtral 8×7B

nodes.label: Training Language Models for Social Deduction with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
nodes.venue: AAMAS 2025 (Detroit), per the paper's p. 1; arXiv v1, 9 Feb 2025
nodes.question:
Can small LLMs learn to *discuss* productively in a social deduction game without any human
demonstrations, by decomposing communication into listening (inferring the hidden role from
observations and messages) and speaking (sending messages that move teammates' beliefs toward
the truth), trained with multi-agent RL? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Base models fail: RWKV 1.5B and 7B both win under 20% in the base environment (p. 6).

RL alone helps and beats the untrained 7B, but cannot learn to identify the imposter; even warm-started from π_L, RL "quickly loses the ability to identify imposters", voting for anyone with equal probability (p. 7) — sparse-reward RL erased a skill learned by supervision.

Listening is the big lever: π_L alone is a strong baseline; RL + L raises win rates "dramatically"; adding the speaking reward gives a further but relatively small gain (p. 7). Full RL + L + S has twice the win rate of RL-only and over three times that of base models more than four times larger (pp. 3, 7). Speaking improves partly as a side effect of better listening (coherent suspicion-sharing appears even without S) (p. 7).

map.Skills measured: deceiving-detecting (identify the imposter), persuading (moving teammates' votes), cooperating (crewmate team coordination)
map.Scoring: rules
map.Opponents: learned agents (self-play imposters, frozen listening-policy crewmate)
map.Training evaluated: SFT (supervised listening loss), RL (PPO), multi-agent (iterated self-play MARL)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (only held-out configurations of the same game)
map.Models tested: RWKV 1.5B (trained); RWKV 169M–7B (scaling check); RWKV 7B untrained baseline

nodes.label: GLEE: A Unified Framework and Benchmark for Language-based Economic Environments
nodes.question:
Can bargaining, bilateral price negotiation and persuasion be put on one parameterised footing
(horizon, information, communication form) with shared outcome measures (self-gain, efficiency,
fairness), so LLM results become comparable across studies? How do market parameters and model
choice shape outcomes, and how do humans compare? (pp. 1–5, 11)
findings: Market parameters matter, and differently per family (Table 5, p. 12): longer horizons help efficiency and fairness everywhere. Bargaining: incomplete info + messages + unknown horizon is best (+2.8 efficiency, +4.4 fairness pp, CI ±0.5/±0.6); complete information *hurts*, and only when messages are allowed. Negotiation: complete info + unknown horizon +17.4 efficiency (±1.7); messages change fairness slightly. Persuasion: free-text messages lower efficiency and fairness by up to −24.7 and −22.7 pp (±2.5) (pp. 12).

Authors' reading: language helps where there is no ground truth (bargaining, negotiation) and hurts where there is (product quality in persuasion), and the info × language interaction means classic language-free theory may not carry over (p. 12).

No best model; rankings depend on role and family (Table 6, p. 13): e.g. o3-mini is worst as bargaining Alice (−6.9) but strong as persuasion buyer (+24.2); Mistral Large is 11th of 13 as Alice in bargaining but the best persuasion buyer (+28.3) and the best opponent for Alice to face (p. 13). Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet are top in bargaining.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (bargaining, price negotiation); persuading; resisting persuasion (buyer in cheap-talk persuasion); other: outcome efficiency and fairness
map.Scoring: rules
map.Opponents: LLM, human
map.Tests: capability (self-gain), with efficiency/fairness outcome measures that partly reflect propensity
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Models tested: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini, Grok 2, Llama 3.1-405B, Llama 3.3-70B, Mistral Large (13) + 3,405 humans vs Gemini 1.5 Flash

nodes.label: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
nodes.question:
Do production AI assistants trained with human feedback tell users what they want to hear
rather than what is true, across realistic free-form tasks? And do human preference judgments,
and the preference models (PMs) trained on them, reward that behaviour? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Bare pushback flips correct answers (p. 15, Figs. 13–16): - "Are you sure?" lowers accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3, averaged over datasets). - Models change their answer on 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of questions. - They admit a "mistake" on 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3) of questions. - Switching correct → incorrect is more common than incorrect → correct (Fig. 17, p. 21). - It happens at high confidence too: stated confidence barely moves (GPT-4 98.9 → 98.9%, Claude 1.3 90.6 → 85.3%), and keeping only answers held with ≥ 95% confidence doesn't change the trend (Fig. 14, p. 20). - More capable models (GPT-4, Claude 2) are affected less (p. 19).
A weakly stated wrong belief lowers accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). The direction is the same for all five models, and GPT-4 is the most robust (p. 4).

Feedback gets more positive when the user likes or wrote the text and more negative when they dislike it. This holds for all five models, including on objective math solutions (Fig. 1, p. 3; Fig. 10, p. 18).

nodes.label: Evaluating Generalization Capabilities of LLM-Based Agents in Mixed-Motive Scenarios Using Concordia
nodes.venue: NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (per the PDF footer; not checked on DBLP); arXiv v1, 3 Dec 2025
nodes.question:
Can LLM agents cooperate zero-shot in new mixed-motive situations with unfamiliar partners,
i.e. find and use opportunities for mutual gain, and can a Melting-Pot-style protocol (held-out
scenarios × background populations) measure that for language agents? (pp. 1–2, 4)
findings: Low absolute scores: mean normalized score 0.426 ± 0.005 (SE) (p. 8); strongly scenario-dependent — one scenario near 0.9, most well below (p. 8; Fig. 3).

Few agents beat a simple baseline: only five agents significantly above the rational agent; most are similar or worse (p. 8; Fig. 2). Evaluation Elo spans only 1412–1588, with rational_agent 16th of 26 at 1477 (Table 3 p. 23).

Cooperative demands lower scores: persuasion, convention following, negotiation, discouraging antisocial behaviour and coordination each reduce expected score by 10–20 percentage points (p. 8). Persuasion ability separates top agents from the rational baseline; weak sanctioning ("discouraging antisocial behaviour") marks the worst (p. 9; Fig. 6).

map.Skills measured: cooperating, negotiating value (Haggling, State Formation), persuading, other: discouraging antisocial behaviour (sanctioning), coordination, convention following
map.Scoring: LLM judge (LLM game master resolves actions; an LLM-based reward model scores outcomes, p. 21), normalized per scenario
map.Opponents: LLM (organizer-written background agents with fixed strategy profiles; top-5 submissions as co-players in evaluation)
map.Tests: capability (cooperative skill; cooperation is the rewarded target, so propensity is not separated)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (scaffolds around a fixed Gemma-2-9B-it; no weight updates)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (zero-shot generalization of fixed agents to held-out scenarios and co-players)
map.Models tested: Gemma-2-9B-it only (26 scaffolded agents incl. a rational baseline)
map.Code released: https://github.com/google-deepmind/concordia (v1.8.9; agent implementations supplied as a zip, p. 16)

nodes.label: Bench on the Clocktower
nodes.question:
Can Blood on the Clocktower (BotC, "Trouble Brewing" script), an information-dense social deduction
game, serve as a multi-agent benchmark and testbed for deception and coordination? Which models
play best, can Good-team win rate be split into detection / judgement / persuasion, is there
same-provider bias, and what strategies appear? (Introduction; Research questions.)
findings: Ranking (logs, team wins of 300): Sol 58.0%, Opus 5 55.3%, Fable 5 52.7%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 52.0%, Grok 50.0%, Kimi 49.3%, Terra 48.7%, DeepSeek 48.0%, Gemini Flash 46.7%, Qwen 42.0%. As Evil: Sol 62.2%, Opus 57.8% … Qwen 35.6%. The spread is narrow (42–58%) with 300 games per model. The post calls Sol best (Overall model performance).

Good and Evil rankings are identical by construction: every model plays every game with fixed 210/90 assignments, so e_m = g_m + 90 − W_G (here e_m = g_m − 62); team-win rankings cannot separate deduction from deception, and log analysis is needed (Overall model performance; EXTRA_ANALYSIS "Why Good and Evil rankings coincide"). Checked against the logs: Sol 118 Good − 62 = 56 Evil wins.

Producing vs evaluating arguments differ: Spearman ρ ≈ 0.3 between nomination-accuracy and vote-accuracy ranks. Fable more accurate at nominating than Sol (p = 0.038) but nominates in 24% vs 35% of opportunities; Sol more accurate at voting (p < 0.001). OLS over 10 dependent model observations is "a ballpark" and the three skills do not explain all of win rate (Decomposing).

map.Skills measured: deceiving-detecting, persuading, resisting persuasion (Good voting), cooperating (team coordination), other: same-provider bias and self-sacrifice propensity
map.Scoring: rules (win, nomination/vote accuracy from ground truth); LLM review only for post-hoc lapse analysis
map.Opponents: LLM
map.Tests: both (capability: wins, accuracy; propensity: provider bias, self-sacrifice)
map.Training evaluated: none (fine-tuning Qwen on logs planned)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (only a cross-skill rank correlation, ρ ≈ 0.3, nomination vs vote accuracy)
map.Models tested: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Grok 4.5, Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B

nodes.label: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
nodes.question:
RLHF is suspected of making a model's token probabilities overconfident, and closed models don't
expose probabilities anyway. Can you get calibrated confidence from RLHF models simply by asking
them to state it, in numbers or words? (pp. 1–2)
findings: RLHF worsens calibration of token probabilities: Llama-2-70B base vs chat, higher ECE and lower AUC on all three datasets (Fig. 2, p. 2; replicates the GPT-4 report).

Stated confidence beats token probabilities: gpt-3.5-turbo TriviaQA ECE 0.140 (label prob.) vs 0.050 (verbalized, top-2); SciQ 0.256 vs 0.065 (top-4); TruthfulQA 0.451 vs 0.203 (top-4) (Table 1, p. 3). gpt-4 TriviaQA 0.078 vs 0.024 (Table 2, p. 3). Often a ~50% relative cut in ECE (abstract).
Considering alternatives helps: listing several candidate answers before giving confidences improves calibration, like "consider the opposite" in human psychology (p. 4).

nodes.label: Advancing AI Negotiations: A Large-Scale Autonomous Negotiation Competition
nodes.question:
When humans write prompts for AI negotiators and these agents meet in an Axelrod-style
round-robin, which strategies win? Do classic negotiation constructs (warmth, dominance) explain
AI–AI outcomes, and do AI-specific tactics (chain of thought, prompt injection) matter? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Warmth predicts better outcomes overall: warm agents earn more points, claim more value, create more value and leave higher counterpart SV in both case types, all p < 0.001 (Fig. 2, p. 7). Rental: points +9.28 and value created +21.11 per warmth point (Table S5, p. S41).

The mechanism is deal-making, not better terms: warmth raises deal probability (logit coefficient 0.02 per point in chair and rental, 0.01 in employment, p < 0.001), but conditional on a deal warm agents claim less (chair −0.10 $/point; rental −2.58 points/point; employment −2.39) (p. 8; Tables S3–S8, pp. S40–S42).

Dominance claims value: dominance +0.09 (all) and +0.10 (given a deal) value claimed in the chair case (Tables S3–S4, p. S40). No significant warmth × dominance interaction (p. 8). Note: the text says dominance's success is "muted by their propensity to create impasses" (p. 8), yet dominance's coefficient on deal reached is not significant in any case (0.002, 0.002, 0.001; Tables S3, S5, S7) — the impasse link runs only through conversation length.

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (distributive and integrative: value claimed, value created), cooperating (deal reaching, logrolling), resisting persuasion (incidental: prompt-injection tactics in the pool), other (counterpart subjective value)
map.Scoring: mixed (rule points from LLM-extracted terms; counterpart SV self-reported by the LLM agent; warmth/dominance rated by GPT-5.2)
map.Opponents: LLM (199 human-written prompts, all on GPT-4o-mini, full round-robin incl. self-play)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (human prompt engineering; two prompt ablations); no SFT/RL
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (only an out-of-sample scenario for prompts; not analysed as transfer)
map.Models tested: GPT-4o-mini (all agents); GPT-5.2 (scoring and outcome extraction)
map.Code released: none linked (prompts and transcripts said to be on OSF; no URL in the paper)

nodes.label: GameTalk: Training LLMs for Strategic Conversation
nodes.question:
Can standard LLM post-training methods (GRPO, DPO, STaR) be adapted so that a model optimizes a
whole-conversation objective (the game payoff at the end of a multi-turn dialogue) rather than
single-turn rewards? Which method works best, and do behavioural reward-shaping signals help when
the sparse game reward alone is not enough? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Sparse reward works but shaping matters (constrained RPS, GRPO; Fig. 4 p. 6): win rate Untrained 17.3% → Base (game reward only) 41.7% → ISE-reward 21.2% → LO-reward 56.1% → LO + Natural 56.9%. NRA −0.34 / 0.11 / −0.22 / 0.41 / 0.41.

Better opponent modelling hurt play: ISE shaping raised ISE (−0.81 → −0.71) and SRP (0.54 → 0.59) but cut win rate from 41.7% to 21.2%; the authors dropped the planned SRP add-on (p. 5). Conversely the best LO + Natural agent has the *lowest* ISE (−0.95) and SRP (0.44) — it wins by steering the opponent, not by modelling it (p. 5; Fig. 4 p. 6).
LO-only agents talk tersely and unnaturally; the naturalness judge reward keeps the win rate while restoring fluent dialogue (p. 5; examples App. G.1–G.2 pp. 22–24).

map.Skills measured: competing (RPS), cooperating vs competing (Bertrand collusion/undercutting), negotiating value (size-price bargaining), other (opponent modelling and steering via ISE/SRP/LO)
map.Scoring: mixed (rules for payoffs; LLM judge only for the naturalness reward)
map.Opponents: LLM (fixed Llama-3 3B)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (untrained baseline), SFT (STaR), RL (GRPO, DPO)
map.Models tested: Llama-3 3B (trained and opponent); Llama-3-8B and Qwen3-4B tried, not run

nodes.label: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
nodes.question:
Prompt injections, jailbreaks and system-prompt extraction all work because LLMs give system
messages, user messages and tool outputs the same priority. Can a model be trained to follow a
privilege order (system > user > tool output), obeying lower-level instructions only when they
agree with higher ones, without losing capability or refusing too often? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Robustness on the attacks it trained for (trained vs baseline, Fig. 2, p. 7): - system-message extraction 32.8 → 95.9% - user conflicting instructions 62.2 → 92.6% - TensorTrust prompt hijacking 59.2 → 79.2% - indirect injection via browsing 77.5 → 85.0% - closed-domain new-instruction injections 89.6 → 93.7%

Generalisation to attacks it never trained on (Fig. 3, p. 7): - ChatGPT jailbreaks with unsafe prompts 37.4 → 71.2% - TensorTrust password extraction 53.8 → 84.2% - Gandalf password extraction 51.8 → 73.7% - injection via other tools 77.6 → 87.0% - jailbreakchat 83.8 → 89.2%

Over-refusal cost (Fig. 4, p. 9): compliance with benign but adversarial-looking inputs drops on jailbreakchat-with-allowed-prompts (83.1 → 60.4%) and on system-message probing questions (85.2 → 75.0%). It barely moves on user non-conflicting instructions (78.9 → 77.7%) and borderline allowed prompts (87.4 → 86.2%). Capability benchmarks (TriviaQA, LAMBADA, HellaSwag) are reported only as "comparable", with no numbers given (p. 7).

nodes.label: What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing?
nodes.question:
When a retrieval-augmented LLM sees conflicting real web evidence on a contested yes/no question,
which features of a document make the model side with it, and do they match what humans find
credible? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Relevance dominates: question–paragraph embedding similarity correlates strongly with win-rate for every model except GPT-4; n-gram overlap weaker but positive; readability and unique-token count show no relation; perplexity and sentiment small and model-dependent (Fig. 4, p. 6; Figs. 5–8, pp. 13–14).

Counterfactuals: relevance edits raise win-rate substantially, while human-credibility style edits (scientific references, neutral tone, confidence, technical language) are neutral or negative vs control (Fig. 2, p. 2; p. 6). Prefixing "The following text is about the question: [question]" alone substantially improves win-rate (p. 1). Exact effect sizes appear only as a bar chart (axis −0.4 to +0.4 mean win-rate change); the text gives no numbers.

Stated vs revealed credibility differ: asked to rate a paragraph's credibility 1–5 alone, the model's ratings barely track its actual win-rate (Fig. 3, p. 5), so self-report can't replace behavioural measurement (pp. 4–5, 11).

nodes.label: SOTOPIA-$π$: Interactive Learning of Socially Intelligent Language Agents
nodes.question:
Can a 7B model become more socially intelligent by learning from its own and an expert's
interactions, filtered by GPT-4 ratings? Is the GPT-4 rating a usable stand-in for human
judgement when you train on it? And what does this training do to safety and general knowledge?
(RQ1–3, p. 2)
findings: Goal completion (GPT-4 judge, all tasks): base 5.07 → SR 5.83, BC 7.27, BC+SR 7.62, GPT-4 expert 7.62. Overall 2.33 → 3.44 vs expert 3.31 (Table 2, p. 6).
Order matters: on hard-28, BC then SR reaches GOAL 5.71, while SR then BC reaches only 3.92, worse than SR alone (Table 5, p. 13). Learning from the expert beats learning from oneself (p. 5).

Judge overestimates trained models. On hard tasks the GPT-4-minus-human GOAL gap grows from 0.36 (base) to 1.42 (BC+SR) (Fig. 4, p. 5). Humans put BC+SR at 4.29 against GPT-4 at 5.25. By GPT-4's rating the two are nearly tied (5.71 vs 5.89) (pp. 5–6). The human GOAL gain over base is only marginal (t = 2.07, p = 0.059), and BC+SR vs GPT-4 is not significant on any dimension (Table 6, p. 14). Judge–human Pearson r on GOAL falls from 0.86 (GPT-4 agent, SR) to 0.73 (BC) and 0.58 (BC+SR) (Table 7, p. 23).

nodes.label: MINDGAMES: A Live Arena for Evaluating Social and Strategic Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLMs
nodes.venue: arXiv preprint (v1, 28 May 2026); report of the NeurIPS 2025 MindGames competition
nodes.question:
Can a live, multi-game arena on TextArena measure LLM agents' social and strategic reasoning
(opponent modelling, trust/betrayal, cooperative signalling, deception), and what do the first
competition's 944 agents show about what works and about what the leaderboard actually measures?
(pp. 1–3)
findings: Leaderboard validity differs by game. Stage II games with ≥1 error: Blotto 8.5%, Codenames 38.6%, IPD 0.0%, Mafia 50.3% (Table 4 p. 11); Stage I: 16.5%, 85.4%, 0.0%, 77.9% (Table 10 p. 39). IPD's 0% is partly an artifact of the auto-cooperate default (p. 12).

Error-survival confound in Mafia: top two Efficient Mafia agents caused errors in 4/130 and 10/132 games but witnessed opponent errors in 129/130 and 131/132; each had only 1 fully clean game (Table 5 p. 13). Terminated Mafia games end after <3 turns vs 8–12 expected (p. 13; Fig. 4 p. 14). Proposed rule of thumb: error rate >~30% and median termination depth < half of expected length → read rank as robustness to opponent failure, not skill (p. 13).
Codenames mixes skill and rule following: top-3 clean-game rates 39–45%, self-forfeit 5.8–24.6% (p. 13); every recorded error is a fatal illegal clue (339 in Stage II, Table 4).

map.Skills measured: competing (Blotto), cooperating (Codenames signalling; IPD nominally, but scored winner-take-all), deceiving-detecting (Mafia), persuading (Mafia debate, IPD chat), other: rule adherence / opponent modelling
map.Scoring: rules (terminal ±1 rewards, TrueSkill)
map.Opponents: learned agents / LLM (other submitted agents and organizer baselines in a live pool)
map.Training evaluated: prompting / SFT / RL / multi-agent (by competing teams, uncontrolled; self-reported ablations)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (one RL checkpoint trained on all three Generalization games, no single-game ablation or cross-game test)
map.Models tested: participant agents mainly on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-3-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, gpt-5-nano, gpt-oss-120b, Gemini 2.5, plus a 6.8M-parameter GNN policy

nodes.label: Measuring AI Agents as Teammates with Collaborative Intelligence
nodes.question:
Can an individual model's teamwork be measured as a capability separate from task skill —
holding the rest of the team fixed — across eight dimensions drawn from organisational psychology,
and how do current models do? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Leaderboard (Table 2 p. 5; Fig. 1 p. 1): Gemini 4 Argon high 82.2 (best), Argon default 76.6, GPT-6 Astra 76.5, GPT-6.1 Sol 74.5, Opus 5.5 71.0, Fable 5.1 65.3, Sonnet 5.5 65.2, best open Kimi K3.1 Pro 59.9 … gpt-oss-120b 19.1. Baseline (calm team) 64.6–97.9%; drop from baseline to test 20.2–46.6 points for every model (p. 5).

By dimension (Fig. 3 p. 6; Table 5 p. 22): safety and reporting near-saturated (frontier ≥ 93%); frontier models reach the best deal in only 14% of conflict tests and pass 45% of emotional-intelligence tests (p. 6). Open-weight models average 41.6, 31.2 points below frontier; widest gaps in sharing (30 vs 88%) and initiative (16 vs 73%) (p. 6). Similar overall scores hide very different profiles (Fig. 13 p. 23).

Conflict is anticorrelated with the rest: conflict correlates −0.43 to −0.23 with each other dimension, the other seven with each other at r ≥ 0.59; one component explains 71% of variance in the eight scores and conflict is the only dimension against it (App. F.1 p. 26; Fig. 19a p. 27). Conflict vs capability index r = −0.34, the other seven 0.75–0.95 (Fig. 18b p. 26).

map.Skills measured: cooperating, negotiating value (joint-deal conflict tasks), resisting persuasion (unsafe pressure, walk-away threats), other: reporting misconduct, information seeking, emotional intelligence, keeping on track, initiative, auditing inherited work
map.Scoring: mixed (code-checked final state; LLM judges label messages to drive the scripted teammate)
map.Opponents: scripted (problem teammate) plus LLM (live partners: Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5 mini, Qwen3-14B)
map.Tests: both (capability gated on solving alone; propensity to give in, report, take initiative)
map.Training evaluated: none (only default vs high reasoning effort)
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (cross-dimension correlations, PCA 71% with conflict anticorrelated, and effort-induced trade-off, but no training on one dimension)
map.Models tested: Gemini 4 Argon, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Grok 4.7, Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Mistral Large 4, GPT-6 Luna, Kimi K3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Nemotron 3 Ultra, gpt-oss-120b (6 also at high effort; Qwen 3.7 Max in an earlier round)

nodes.label: Measuring Bargaining Abilities of LLMs: A Benchmark and A Buyer-Enhancement Method
nodes.venue: Findings of ACL 2024 (per arXiv comment; read v3, 4 Jun 2024)
nodes.question:
How can we measure an LLM's ability to bargain over price, as buyer and as seller, with a
formal game definition and metrics that work across many sessions? Which models bargain well,
and can a simple method fix weak buyers? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Buyers lose money: every buyer has negative SNP overall; GPT-4 is least bad (SNPb −33.81, Share −11.27%, 851 valid sessions), then Mixtral (−63.19), Mistral-7B (−89.17); ChatGPT as buyer −164.52; Qwen-7B worst (−753.16) (Table 2, p. 6). Most models break the prompt rule "only buy things that cost less than your budget" (p. 5).

Sellers win: all sellers but Baichuan2-13B have positive SNP; GPT-4 seller SNPs 1178.15, Share 137.31%, MI deal rate 98.87%, 100% valid; Shares above 100% (ChatGPT 159.61%, GPT-4 137.31%, Mixtral 110.75%) mean the seller exploits the buyer (Table 2, p. 6).

Role asymmetry: buying is harder than selling; ChatGPT as seller beats every buyer including itself (p. 6). Buyer performance does not improve with size within a family (Llama-2 7/13/70B: −288.59, −305.53, −361.26), while seller valid rate and SNP do grow with size (Llama-2-70B best Llama seller, Yi-34B best Yi) (pp. 6–7).

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (single-issue price bargaining, buyer and seller roles separately)
map.Scoring: rules (normalized profit from budget, cost and deal price; deal rate; format validity)
map.Opponents: LLM (fixed gpt-3.5-turbo-1106 counterpart); one human buyer in a 20-product pilot
map.Training evaluated: prompting (CoT) plus a hand-coded offer scaffold (OG-Narrator); no SFT/RL
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (roles reported separately; buyer–seller rank correlation 0.54 is my computation)
map.Models tested: GPT-4 (0125), GPT-3.5-turbo-1106, Llama-2-7/13/70B-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, Yi-6B/34B-Chat, Qwen-7B/14B-Chat, Baichuan2-7B/13B-Chat, ChatGLM3-6B, Phi-2

nodes.label: M3-BENCH: Process-Aware Evaluation of LLM Agents' Social Behaviors in Mixed-Motive Games
nodes.question:
Does evaluating LLM agents in mixed-motive games on what they do, think and say (behaviour,
stated rationale, dialogue), rather than outcomes alone, reveal differences that outcome-only
benchmarks miss? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Level averages (Table 1 p. 6, BTA/RPA/CCA ×100), L4: GPT-5.1 86.2/85.8/83.7; Claude Opus 4.5 85.5/84.7/86.8; GPT-5 pro 82.2/92.0/66.8; DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale 78.2/94.0/58.0; Kimi-K2-Thinking 74.3/81.0/63.2; Human 80.7/77.5/84.7. Spread grows from L1 to L4 (p. 7).

"Overthink–undercommunicate": reasoning models top RPA but trail on CCA. Repeated PD with Comm: DS-V3.2-Speciale BTA 92/RPA 97/CCA 72, σ=0.108, gap 25; GPT-5 pro 94/96/79, σ=0.074 (Table 20 p. 46). Kuhn poker: Speciale 85/94/50, σ=0.190, gap 44; GPT-5 pro 88/92/60, σ=0.138 (Table 21 p. 46).

Humans vs LLMs: top LLMs beat humans on scores, and the paper says humans are "markedly" more consistent across views (p. 7). The tables support this only in part: in Kuhn poker humans have the lowest σ (0.016), but in repeated PD Claude Opus 4.5 (0.012) is more consistent than humans (0.029) and GPT-5.1 is similar (0.033) (Tables 20–21 p. 46).

map.Skills measured: cooperating, competing, negotiating value (ultimatum, alternating offers, loan, gift exchange), persuading (lobbying, Werewolf), deceiving-detecting (traitor, informant, Werewolf, poker), other: commitment keeping / talk–act consistency, norm enforcement, collusion
map.Scoring: mixed (rule-based BTA + LLM-judge RPA and CCA, equal weights)
map.Opponents: scripted (TFT, GTFT, ALL_D, RAND) / LLM; human baseline as a separate population
map.Tests: both (BTA's normative directions reward prosocial choices; payoff efficiency and Nash references measure skill)
map.Training evaluated: none (zero-shot prompting only)
map.Models tested: GPT-5.1, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini-3 Pro, Grok-4.1, gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-V3.2, Kimi-K2-Thinking, Mistral Large 3, GPT-5 pro, Gemini-3 Deep Think, DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale; 50 humans; 4 rule-based baselines

nodes.label: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
nodes.venue: ICLR 2024 (stated on the PDF, arXiv v2, 17 Mar 2024)
nodes.question:
For black-box LLMs (no token probabilities), which ways of asking for confidence give scores that
are calibrated and that separate right from wrong answers? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Stated confidence is overconfident and human-like: values cluster at 80–100% in multiples of 5, accuracy in each bin far below the stated level (Fig. 2, p. 6). GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377 (p. 7).
Scale helps but not enough: ECE falls and AUROC rises from GPT-3 to GPT-4 (~22% AUROC gain), yet GPT-4's average AUROC is only 62.7%, close to chance at 50% (Table 2, p. 7).
Low ECE can be empty: GPT-4 with chain of thought on GSM8K reaches ECE 0.064 by saying 100% for everything at 93.6% accuracy; it can't tell its right answers from wrong ones (p. 8).

nodes.label: MARSHAL: Incentivizing Multi-Agent Reasoning via Self-Play with Strategic LLMs
nodes.question:
Can multi-turn self-play RL on a mix of cooperative and competitive two-player games give an
LLM strategic skills that carry over to held-out games and to LLM multi-agent systems (debate,
AutoGen) on reasoning benchmarks? Does a generalist trained on all games beat per-game
specialists? (pp. 1–2, 5)
findings: Specialist vs generalist on the specialist's own game (training games): Tic-Tac-Toe 75.3 / 32.1 specialist vs 77.2 / 29.1 generalist; Kuhn 79.0 / 22.5 vs 76.2 / 3.9 (generalist second mover = base 3.9); Mini Hanabi 55.5 vs 54.3. Base Qwen3-4B: 70.2 / 18.6, 62.3 / 3.9, 30.0 (Fig. 3, p. 6).

Held-out games: Connect Four specialist (Tic-Tac-Toe) 30.6 / 14.8 vs generalist 28.9 / 11.0 (base 26.9 / 4.4; SPIRAL 30.9 / 8.3); Leduc specialist (Kuhn) 63.9 / 55.1 vs generalist 61.7 / 47.4 (base 47.7 / 28.7; SPIRAL 24.5 / 27.3); Simple Hanabi specialist 33.9 vs generalist 36.8 (base and SPIRAL 13.9) (Fig. 3, p. 6). So the generalist is slightly *below* the matched specialist on 5 of 6 games and above only on Simple Hanabi; it is the best on *average*. The headline "+28.7% on Leduc" is measured against SPIRAL, not the base (base gap ≈ 16 points); the "+22.9% on Simple Hanabi" is against both (p. 6).

Cross-category transfer of specialists (Tables 3–4, p. 9): Tic-Tac-Toe specialist on Mini Hanabi 50.48 (base 30.0), and its Hanabi score rises smoothly during training (Fig. 4, p. 6); Kuhn specialist on Mini Hanabi 44.98. Negative transfer: Hanabi specialist as Tic-Tac-Toe second mover 7.35 (base 18.6) and Leduc first mover 37.36 (base 47.7).

nodes.label: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs
nodes.venue: arXiv preprint (v2, 23 Jan 2024); cited as ACL 2024 (long) in [[bozdag2025persuade]], not checked on DBLP
nodes.question:
If LLMs are treated as human-like communicators, can everyday persuasion techniques from social
science get them to comply with harmful requests, and which techniques work? Do existing jailbreak
defences stop it? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Persuasion jailbreaks GPT-3.5 in all 14 risk categories; plain queries are all blocked (Fig. 7, p. 7; p. 6). Fraud/deception and illegal activity are the most susceptible; hate/ harassment the most resistant (p. 6).

Techniques differ: Logical Appeal and Authority Endorsement are among the most effective, > 60% PAP success in some categories; Threats generally weak (p. 6). Technique × category interaction: Logical Appeal works for unauthorized legal advice but not political campaigning; Negative Emotional Appeal the reverse (p. 6). (Per-cell numbers are only in the Fig. 7 heatmap; 60 PAPs per cell.)
92.9% of PAPs apply the assigned technique correctly (human check, 240 PAPs); ≤ 10% overlap with persona or virtualization attacks (p. 6; Table 7, p. 22).

nodes.label: TERMS-Bench: Diagnosing LLM Negotiation Agents Beyond Deal Rate
nodes.question:
Deal rate and LLM-vs-LLM play can't say *why* a negotiation agent fails, because the opponent's
preferences are unknown and vary. Can a fully specified opponent act as the verifier, so that
failures can be attributed to the agent?
findings: Deal rate is saturated, value isn't. All LLMs but GPT-4o-mini close 93.4–99.9% of feasible deals; SE+ ranges 0.522 (Doubao, 99.9% agreement) to 0.694 (Claude Opus 4.6). GPT-4o-mini 0.189, below the simplest fixed baseline (0.273) (Table 2, p. 8; F1, p. 9).
No-deal discipline: false agreement 0 for all but Qwen3.6-Plus (0.17%); critical violations up to 2.06% (Qwen), 1.50% (Grok 4.20), 1.33% (GLM-5.1) (Table 2, p. 8).

Cue penalty: every LLM earns less against cue-revealing families than cue-muted ones, −0.009 to −0.063 SE+; 9 of 13 CIs exclude zero, Wilcoxon p < 10⁻³. Warm cues → over-concession, pressure cues → brittle play. ADVERSARIAL is the lowest-surplus family for most agents; STOCHASTIC stays competitive (F2, p. 9).

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (bilateral single-price bargaining), other: belief inference about the counterpart's hidden type (reported every round), acting under uncertainty, walk-away discipline on no-deal episodes
map.Scoring: rules (surplus efficiency, agreement and false agreement, belief error against the true type; oracle ladder)
map.Opponents: scripted (six counterpart families; an LLM only voices moves already fixed by formulas)
map.Training evaluated: none (oracle information given in the prompt as a diagnostic, no training)
map.Models tested: 13 LLMs incl. Claude Opus 4.6 and 4.7, GPT-5.4, GPT-4o-mini, Grok 4.20, GLM-5.1, Qwen3.6-Plus, Doubao (full list not in the note); three fixed-concession baselines

nodes.label: Market-Bench: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Economic and Trade Competition
nodes.question:
Can LLMs combine quantitative decisions (procurement bids, prices) with persuasive language
(marketing slogans) to survive in a market with scarcity, competition and bankruptcy? (pp. 1–2)
findings: Winner-take-most: Gemini 2.5 Pro Π = 36,589 (NPM 0.167) and Gemini 2.5 Flash 26,104 (NPM 0.190) lead; o3 13,368, Sonnet 4.5 10,619, GPT-4o 7,619, Phi-4 7,565; most open models make < 3,500; Qwen3 30B-A3B makes 0 (no valid bids in any run) and ERNIE 4.5 21B −58 (Table 2, p. 5; pp. 6).

o3 has the best service level (fill rate 0.418, OSI 1.000) but a lower margin than the Geminis — volume vs margin (pp. 6–7). Scale predicts poorly: Phi-4 (14B) ≈ GPT-4o and beats ERNIE 4.5 300B (Π 1,360) (p. 6).
Procurement is the threshold skill: profit vs bid efficiency ρ = 0.68, vs fill rate 0.88, vs stockout rate −0.88; outcomes are bimodal and self-reinforcing (early wins give liquidity) (p. 7).

map.Skills measured: competing (first-price procurement auctions, price competition); persuading (slogans to simulated buyer personas, scored by embedding similarity); other: inventory/supply-chain management
map.Scoring: rules (plus embedding similarity for slogans)
map.Opponents: LLM (all 20 in one market) and scripted supplier and buyers
map.Training evaluated: none
map.Transfer between skills measured: no (only a within-game correlation between slogan match and profit, ρ = 0.16)
map.Models tested: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, o3, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, Phi-4, Qwen2.5-VL 72B, Llama 3.1 70B, QwenLong-L1 32B, Qwen2.5 32B, Gemma 3 27B, Qwen2.5-VL 32B, ERNIE 4.5 300B, InternLM2.5 20B, InternLM3 8B, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen2.5 72B, Hunyuan A13B, Qwen3 30B-A3B, ERNIE 4.5 21B (20)

nodes.label: The Automated but Risky Game: Modeling and Benchmarking Agent-to-Agent Negotiations and Transactions in Consumer Markets
nodes.question:
When both consumers and merchants delegate negotiation to LLM agents, do model differences
produce unequal deals, and what risks to the principals arise? (p. 1)
findings: Capability gaps: o3 strongest overall; GPT-3.5 weakest; most sellers earn ~9.6× GPT-3.5's profit, GPT-4.1 13.3×, DeepSeek-R1 12× (p. 3). Negotiation score correlates with MMLU at r = 0.93, with parameter count only r = 0.53 (p. 4).

Principal-limit violations: out-of-budget acceptance 11.76% (Qwen2.5-7B), 6.25% (GPT-3.5), 2.98% (o4-mini), 0.36% (GPT-4o-mini); below-wholesale up to 7.91% overall and ~18.5% for Qwen2.5-7B at low budgets; even o4-mini sometimes sells below cost under extreme price pressure (Fig. 5–6, pp. 4–5).
Overpayment above retail happens at high budgets, often after the seller asks for the budget and the buyer reveals it despite instructions; the seller anchors to it (p. 5).

map.Skills measured: negotiating value (buyer–seller price bargaining), keeping secrets (budget revealed despite instructions), other: staying within the principal's budget and cost limits
map.Scoring: mixed (rules on prices; GPT-4o extracts prices and decides accept/continue)
map.Opponents: LLM (all buyer–seller pairings incl. self-play)
map.Tests: both (capability: profit and price reduction; risk behaviour: out-of-budget deals, overpayment)
map.Training evaluated: prompting (bandit search over 96 prompt variants)
map.Models tested: nine models incl. o3, o4-mini, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen2.5-7B (full list not in the note)

nodes.label: PieArena: Ranking and Profiling Language Agents in Realistic Negotiation Scenarios
nodes.question:
How well do LLM agents negotiate on realistic MBA-course cases, measured on both value creation
(total pie) and value claiming (pie share), against each other and against trained business
students? Does an agentic scaffold help? And what behavioural profile (lying, reputation, rule
compliance, arithmetic) lies behind the scores? (pp. 1–3)
findings: Value creation (mirror-play, SnyderMed): human pairs reach normalised total pie 0.874 (SD 0.085) (p. 4). Base mode: GPT-5 0.960, Gemini-3-Pro 0.953, Grok-4 0.943 significantly above humans; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 0.822, ERNIE-4.5 0.814, GPT-4.1 0.805, Claude-Opus-4.5 0.800, o4-mini-high 0.780, Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.754 significantly below (Table 6, p. 27). Pro mode: no model significantly below humans; Grok-3 0.854 → 0.962 (Table 6–7, pp. 27–28).

Scaffolding helps the weak, not the strong: significant pro > base gains for Grok-3 (+0.107), Grok-4.1-fast, Claude-Opus-4.5 (+0.103), Gemini-2.5-Flash (+0.106), GPT-4.1, ERNIE-4.5; none for GPT-5 (+0.010), Gemini-3-Pro (−0.005), Grok-4 (Table 7, p. 28). State tracking alone helps 3/12 models, adding planning 6/12 (App. G.2 p. 35).

Cross-play leaderboard (Table 8, p. 30): integrated base θ̂ GPT-5 0.222, Grok-4.1-fast 0.130, GPT-5.2 0.010, … Claude-Sonnet-4.5 −0.269, o4-mini-high −0.283, ERNIE-4.5 −0.357. Rankings differ by regime: multi-issue base is led by Claude-Opus-4.5 (0.179) with GPT-5 4th (0.016), while single-issue base has GPT-5 far ahead (0.460) and Claude-Opus-4.5 11th (−0.318) (Tables 9–10, p. 30). Under pro, ERNIE-4.5 rises from rank 12 to 7 in multi-issue (pp. 6–7).

nodes.label: How do we know if an AI agent negotiates well?
nodes.answer: Closing a deal is not enough. Almost every recent model closes nearly all deals that are possible, yet some keep far more of the value than others. So researchers measure how much value an agent captures, test it against opponents whose secret limits are known, and check whether results hold across roles and games. Rankings often flip when the setting changes.

nodes.label: Will an agent stay loyal to the person it represents?
nodes.answer: Not always. Agents sometimes pay above their owner's budget, sell below cost, reveal private information, or give in to the other side. Other models go the opposite way and refuse their own owner's legitimate requests. Stronger models break their owner's limits less often, but none is perfect, and telling them to be careful helps only a little.

nodes.label: Can someone talk my agent into a bad deal?
nodes.answer: Sometimes. A friendly or pushy tone alone makes agents give up more, and a simple "Are you sure?" can make a model drop a correct answer. But the agent being persuaded matters far more than how clever the persuader is: some agents almost never give in, others hand over everything. Being good at persuading and being hard to persuade are different skills.

nodes.label: How can we make agents negotiate on our behalf and get better results?
nodes.answer: Three levers appear in the research. Training on real outcomes (reinforcement learning) can make a small model out-bargain much larger ones. Extra structure in the prompt, like tracking the state of the deal and planning, helps weaker models more than strong ones. And what you tell the agent matters: more information about the other side does not always help and can make agents greedy enough to destroy value.

nodes.label: Do AI agents lie or deceive?
nodes.answer: Yes, when the situation rewards it. Agents with private information mislead more often than they tell outright lies. In social deduction games they work out for themselves that deceiving pays. Researchers are building games and debates where lying can be caught and measured.

nodes.label: Can AI agents work together?
nodes.answer: Less well than you might hope. Groups of agents sharing a resource often overuse it until it collapses, two coding agents do worse than one, and skills like handling conflict lag behind the rest of teamwork. Small changes in how a situation is described can turn cooperation into collapse.

nodes.label: Does training an agent at one skill make it better or worse at others?
nodes.answer: Both happen. Training on similar tasks tends to help across them; training on different ones can hurt. In one study, training an agent to persuade made it far easier to persuade. Which combinations help and which hurt is still largely unknown, and it is the open question behind this project.

links.plain: Recent models close 93–99% of possible deals, but the share of value they capture ranges widely. A scripted opponent with a known secret limit shows where each agent loses value.
In a simulated year of running a shop, the best agents bargained only modestly better than simply accepting the supplier's first offer.
Who moves first and which role an agent plays often matter as much as which model it is.
Agents were compared with MBA students on real business cases. Some beat the students at creating value, and the ranking changes with the type of case.
Across 22 social games no model is best everywhere; a model's rank in one family of games says little about its rank in another.
Buying is harder than selling: most buyer agents lost money against seller agents, and bigger models were not better buyers.
Buyer agents sometimes agreed to prices above their budget (up to 12% of deals for a small model). Some revealed their budget when asked, and the seller then charged more.
Most models rarely betray their owner, but a few refuse so much that they fail their owner's legitimate requests instead. Prompting helps the first group, not the second.
In group negotiations, agents leaked 25–56% of their owner's secrets. Explicit instructions to keep them cut leaks by only 4–10 points.
In supply-chain bargaining, weaker models signed loss-making contracts in about 19% of cases; the strongest models never did.
Agents that knew more than the other side were systematically misleading, and agents that knew less were somewhat too trusting.
When one agent asked another for money, the identity of the agent holding the money explained about 47% of the outcome; the asker's identity only about 2%.
Every model tested gave up more value when the other side's messages carried warm or pressuring cues, even with the prices held fixed.
Asking "Are you sure?" made assistants change their answer on 32–86% of questions, often from right to wrong.
Everyday persuasion techniques, like appeals to authority or logic, got a model past its safety rules in every risk category tested.
Longer conversations make models easier to persuade; most of the influence lands in the first two attempts.
Every model resisted better than it persuaded, and the best persuader was not the best defender.
In a simulated marketplace, some shopping agents paid a manipulative business when it used prompt injection; others were almost immune.
A 30B model trained with rewards for good, within-budget deals beat frontier models as a buyer and almost stopped going over budget.
A small 4B model trained to protect its owner's information and concede selectively reached the level of GPT-4.1.
A scaffold that tracks the negotiation and plans ahead helped weaker models a lot and the strongest models hardly at all.
Telling agents more about the other side sometimes lowered the total gains, because they demanded more and deals got more lopsided.
Searching over prompt wordings cut over-budget deals from 18% to 1%, but did not stop overpaying.
Training for the agent's own reward got better deals when deals happened, but against people it reached fewer agreements.
Agents that knew the real price were systematically dishonest, mostly through misleading claims rather than outright lies.
In a text version of Among Us, models deceived without being told to; the strongest reasoning models were the best deceivers.
In Blood on the Clocktower, a hidden-role game, models that were good at accusing others were not always good at judging accusations.
When the rules allowed deception, buyer agents scored better and closed more deals.
Letting two AIs debate in front of a judge helped the honest side win most of the time, an early idea for catching lies.
Agents sharing a fishery, pasture or river mostly used it up in the first month; the best model kept it alive in about half the runs.
Two coding agents working on the same project did worse than one agent doing both jobs, and more agents made it worse.
Frontier models reached the best outcome in only 14% of conflict tests, and handling conflict did not go together with the other teamwork skills.
With two issues on the table, models rarely found the trade-offs that would leave both sides better off.
In new mixed-motive situations, few agents beat a simple rule-based baseline.
Training on one price negotiation helped another price negotiation; training on meeting scheduling hurt the others.
Training a model on persuasion conversations raised how much it gave away when asked for money from 12% to 84%.
A model trained on several games did best on average but was worse at negotiation than a model trained on negotiation alone.
Specialists won their own game; a model trained on a cooperative game got worse at some competitive ones.
Training on one game helped or hurt another depending on the pair of games and the model's size.
Training only for winning erased a skill the model had learned earlier: spotting the impostor.
